quote: The mistake is in thinking that, if the particular path that was chosen yields statistical significance, this is strong evidence in favor of the hypothesis.

title: Preregistration helps in some fields but is not a general fix
guidance: Gelman and Loken endorse preregistration where new data are cheap to collect, but argue that in applied observational work on familiar public data the most valuable analyses arise iteratively, so preregistration cannot be the universal remedy. For observational management fields the realistic alternatives are analysis of all relevant comparisons and clear exploratory versus confirmatory labelling.
action: When evaluating an observational field, do not treat absence of preregistration as disqualifying; instead ask whether the full set of comparisons was analysed and reported.
quote: Preregistration may be practical in some fields and for some types of problems, but it cannot realistically be a general solution.

title: Analyze all relevant comparisons, not only the significant ones
guidance: Where preregistration and replication are infeasible, the authors recommend analysing the full set of relevant comparisons rather than reporting the one that happened to be significant, possibly using multilevel modelling to handle the multiplicity. This is the intellectual root of multiverse and specification-curve reporting.
action: Where a field relies on observational data, favour studies that report the full specification space over studies that report a single favoured comparison.
quote: A starting point would be to analyze all relevant comparisons, not just focusing on whatever happens to be statistically significant.

title: Multiplicity of analysis strategies acceptable by field standards
guidance: For a given research question there is usually great flexibility in the analysis strategy, and many of the possible strategies are acceptable by the scientific standards of the field. The problem is therefore not deviation from standards but the breadth of what standards permit.
action: For each design on the map, list the alternative strategies a competent analyst in the field could have chosen at each step; this set defines the multiverse.
quote: there is usually great flexibility in the choice of analysis strategy, as many possible strategies are acceptable according to the scientific standards of the field

title: Multiplicity plus selective reporting inflates effects and false positives
guidance: The authors summarise evidence that combining a multiplicity of analysis strategies with selective reporting systematically increases false-positive results, inflates effect sizes and produces overoptimistic measures of predictive performance. Ignoring multiplicity yields overconfidence in precision and findings that do not replicate.
action: When only one specification is reported from a large plausible set, treat the reported precision as overstated and the effect size as likely inflated.
quote: the combination of this multiplicity with selective reporting can systematically lead to an increase in false-positive results, inflated effect sizes and overoptimistic measures of predictive performance

title: Imprecise hypotheses leave variable definitions to the analyst
guidance: Flexibility in data preprocessing arises partly because research hypotheses are not precise enough to fully specify the input and outcome variables; meat consumption can mean all meat, red meat, or specific species, and the outcome can be colon, rectal or all colorectal cancer. Each definition is a defensible but consequential choice.
action: Record how each theoretical construct was operationalized and whether the hypothesis as stated would have permitted other definitions.
quote: the research hypotheses are generally not precise enough that they fully specify the input and the outcome variables

title: No clear rule separates mandatory controls from needless complexity
guidance: In explanatory modelling the aim is to control for all confounders, but the candidate list is never exhaustive and there is no clear guidance on which variables are mandatory and which merely complicate the model. Control selection is therefore an unavoidable fork in the analysis.
action: Treat the control set as a specification choice to be varied, and note which controls the field considers mandatory versus discretionary.
quote: there is no clear guidance on which variables should be considered mandatory in the model and which will lead to an unnecessarily complex description of the phenomenon of interest

title: Justifiable paths lead to different results; that variability is real
guidance: Although some analytic choices could be called wrong, many are justifiable, and because all justifiable paths are likely to produce different results there is a source of variability attributable to the analysis strategy. This variability is rarely accounted for or discussed when results are presented.
action: Distinguish wrong from justifiable choices when building a multiverse, keep only the justifiable ones, and report the variability across them as part of the result.
quote: As all justifiable paths are likely to lead to different results, we see there is a source of variability attributable to the choice of analysis strategy

title: Four epistemic sources: preprocessing, parameter, model and method
guidance: The framework traces multiplicity to four sources: data preprocessing uncertainty (selection, definition, cleaning and transformation of variables), model uncertainty (the true model structure is unknown), parameter uncertainty (values that must be specified without theory or measurement), and method uncertainty (which estimation or computational method to use).
action: Organise the forking paths of a design under these four headings so that gaps in coverage become visible.
quote: Data preprocessing uncertainty is caused by all decisions needing to be made in the selection of the data to analyse and in the definition, the cleaning and the transformation of the input and the outcome variables

title: Epistemic uncertainty arises from lack of knowledge, not randomness
guidance: Preprocessing, parameter, model and method uncertainty are epistemic: they stem from a lack of knowledge about the right specification, and are contrasted with measurement and sampling uncertainty, which are random and produce variability when the same strategy is applied to different data. A map of assumptions should separate the two kinds.
action: Tag each uncertainty on the map as epistemic (specification choice) or random (sampling, measurement), since they call for different remedies.
quote: The uncertainties detailed above—data preprocessing uncertainty, parameter uncertainty, model uncertainty and method uncertainty—are epistemic: they arise due to a lack of knowledge.

title: Confidence intervals capture only sampling uncertainty
guidance: In explanatory modelling the reported confidence intervals and tests account only for sampling uncertainty and ignore measurement and epistemic uncertainty, giving apparently precise results that are not robust to the choice of analysis strategy and have a high probability of being contradicted in replication.
action: Read a reported confidence interval as a lower bound on total uncertainty and ask what the interval would look like across the plausible specification set.
quote: confidence intervals and hypothesis tests typically only account for sampling uncertainty, while ignoring measurement and epistemic uncertainty

title: Transparency alone does not prevent selective reporting
guidance: Publishing data, code and materials builds trust and efficiency but only indirectly addresses multiplicity, and is not enough on its own to prevent selective reporting or overconfidence; likewise no inferential paradigm, including confidence intervals or Bayes factors, is immune to result-dependent selection of a strategy. The sources of uncertainty must be addressed explicitly.
action: Give credit for open data and code, but do not let it substitute for evidence that the reported specification was not selected on its result.
quote: Transparency alone is again not enough to prevent selective reporting or eliminate overconfidence in results

title: Precise theory shrinks the multiverse
guidance: Among strategies to reduce uncertainty, Steegen and colleagues and Schaller call for more conceptual rigour and more precise theories so that fewer analysis strategies are admissible; benchmarking studies can similarly reduce method uncertainty by identifying a best method for a setting.
action: When a theory is vague about operationalization or functional form, note that the multiverse is correspondingly large and ask whether the theory could be sharpened to prune it.
quote: call for more conceptual rigour and precise theories to reduce the number of possible analysis strategies

title: Readers can run robustness checks when data are public
guidance: Reporting approaches such as vibration of effects, specification curve, multiverse and multimodel analysis assess robustness to alternative assumptions, and where data are public these methods can be applied by readers and reviewers to test whether the originally reported results survive alternative analysis choices.
action: Where a focal study's data are available, treat an independent specification-curve run as a feasible next step and record its result on the map.
quote: methods to report uncertainty can be applied by readers and reviewers to assess to what extent the originally reported results are robust to alternative analysis choices

title: Confirmatory status requires pre-specification or blinding
guidance: Strictly confirmatory analyses are possible only when the analysis strategy is specified in detail before the data are observed, through preregistration or registered reports, or when the analyst is blinded to the outcome while choosing the strategy; split analysis plans in algorithmic modelling serve the same purpose.
action: Classify each reported test as confirmatory only if a preregistration, registered report, blind analysis or holdout split is documented; otherwise label it exploratory.
quote: Strictly confirmatory analyses can be realized either through the pre-registration of analysis plans [93,94] and registered reports [95], where the analysis strategy is specified in detail before observing the data

title: Six steps: be aware, reduce, integrate, report, acknowledge, publish
guidance: Table 2 lists six steps for an individual researcher: before analysis, be aware of the multiplicity and reduce sources of uncertainty in the design; during analysis, integrate remaining uncertainty and report results of alternative strategies; after analysis, acknowledge the inherent uncertainty and publish all code, data and material.
action: Use the six steps as a checklist when auditing a design, scoring which were visibly carried out.
quote: (1) be aware of the multiplicity of possible analysis strategies

title: With administrative data, epistemic uncertainty dwarfs sampling uncertainty
guidance: As research increasingly uses data not recorded for research purposes, such as administrative, routine-care or remote-sensing data, sampling uncertainty becomes comparatively small while measurement, preprocessing, model and method uncertainty become much larger than with designed experiments. Standard errors will understate uncertainty even more in these settings.
action: For designs built on large archival or administrative datasets, prioritise mapping specification and measurement assumptions over sampling precision.
quote: sampling uncertainty, which has attracted a disproportionate amount of attention in the scientific community to this point, will be comparably small, but measurement, data preprocessing, model and method uncertainty will be much larger

title: Multiverses mislead when included choices are not truly arbitrary
guidance: Multiverse-style methods presuppose that the alternative specifications are arbitrary or equally reasonable. If some alternatives are in fact better justified, the multiverse can hide a genuine effect in a mass of poorly justified specifications and produce misleading robustness conclusions.
action: Before accepting a multiverse result as evidence of fragility, check whether the authors justified each decision node as genuinely arbitrary.
quote: if specifications are not truly arbitrary, multiverse-style analyses can produce misleading results, potentially hiding meaningful effects within a mass of poorly justified alternatives

title: Preregistration does not guarantee representative or robust specifications
guidance: A preregistered analysis plan limits p-hacking, but the single preregistered specification may still be unrepresentative of the set of valid specifications. Preregistration and multiverse analysis therefore address different problems and one does not substitute for the other.
action: Record preregistration status and specification robustness as separate attributes of a study's evidence rather than treating preregistration as proof of robustness.
quote: Although preregistration limits the scope for p-hacking and similar questionable practices, it does not guarantee that the chosen specifications are representative and robust

title: Theory-justified choices should not generate multiverse alternatives
guidance: A choice that theory or background knowledge clearly favours over alternatives is nonarbitrary, and Simonsohn and colleagues likewise exclude unambiguously inferior specifications. Only choices with no objective justification for one option over another belong in the multiverse.
action: Separate each design choice in the field into justified-by-theory versus arbitrary before deciding what to vary in a multiverse.
quote: any choice that theory or background knowledge indicates is clearly justified over others is nonarbitrary and should not be used to generate alternative specifications

title: Different covariate sets answer different questions, not robustness
guidance: Quoting Simonsohn and colleagues, the authors note that analyses with and without a set of covariates estimate different quantities, so covariate selection should not usually be part of robustness tests. Published applications such as vibration of effects have nevertheless varied only covariates, revealing a lack of conceptual consensus.
action: Treat alternative control sets as alternative estimands; do not fold them into a single robustness multiverse without a causal argument.
quote: with and without a certain set of covariates are not different answers to the same question, they are different answers to different questions

title: Combinatorial explosion drowns justified specifications
guidance: A few decision nodes wrongly treated as arbitrary multiply the multiverse quickly: five binary nodes expand it 32-fold, so if one option is justified at each node, justified specifications occupy only 3 percent of the multiverse, and 0.4 percent with three-way nodes. Summary statistics such as the median effect then become meaningless.
action: Count how many decision nodes were varied and estimate what fraction of specifications would survive a principled filter before interpreting a median or mean effect.
quote: Just a few decisions incorrectly treated as arbitrary can quickly explode the size of the multiverse, drowning reasonable effect estimates in a sea of unjustified alternatives.

title: Three kinds of a priori nonequivalence among specifications
guidance: The framework distinguishes measurement nonequivalence (alternatives differ in validity or reliability), effect nonequivalence (alternatives estimate different effects, for example because covariates change the estimand) and power/precision nonequivalence (alternatives differ in sample size or precision). Other domains such as outlier rules and model choice also apply but are not exhaustive.
action: For every decision node in a multiverse, ask whether the alternatives differ in measurement validity, in the effect estimated, or in precision; if so, they are not arbitrary.
quote: Specifically, we consider measurement nonequivalence, effect nonequivalence, and power/precision nonequivalence.

title: Alternative measures with different validity are not interchangeable
guidance: When a construct could be measured in several ways, the choice of measure becomes a decision node, but different measures often differ predictably in validity and reliability, with predictable consequences for the estimated effect. Such alternatives cannot be treated as equivalent branches of a multiverse.
action: Document the validity evidence for each proxy used in the field and rank proxies rather than treating all of them as arbitrary choices.
quote: different measurement choices can often be expected to yield systematic differences in validity and reliability, with predictable consequences on the effect of interest

title: Composites of valid indicators predictably outperform single items
guidance: Unless a composite contains many invalid indicators, it will have higher validity than individual indicators, which translates into larger effects, more precise estimates and higher power. A multiverse that mixes single items and composites, as in the adolescent well-being study with more than 15,000 short scales, therefore builds predictable heterogeneity into the results.
action: Flag multiverses that vary the number of items or indicators as measurement-nonequivalent and do not read their spread as instability of the effect.
quote: it will generally yield a higher validity than individual indicators—which translates into larger effect sizes, more precise estimates, and higher statistical power

title: Covariate selection is a causal-model question, not a robustness knob
guidance: Whether including a variable adds or removes bias depends on its role in the causal model, for example confounder, mediator or collider. Covariate choice is therefore fundamentally theoretical, and alternative covariate sets should not be pooled within one multiverse because they estimate different, sometimes mutually incompatible, effects.
action: Draw or elicit the field's implicit causal graph and classify each control as confounder, mediator or collider before judging whether a specification's controls are appropriate.
quote: The impact of including versus excluding a given variable depends on the role played by that variable in the causal model that (explicitly or implicitly) underlies the analysis

title: Effects changing with mediators or confounders is expected, not instability
guidance: In the vibration-of-effects demonstration, all combinations of 13 covariates were used even though many of them are plausibly mediators or confounders of the predictor. Estimates are expected to change, sometimes dramatically, when such variables are controlled, so this variation does not indicate a fragile result.
action: When a specification curve shows large shifts tied to particular controls, check whether those controls are mediators or confounders before describing the effect as non-robust.
quote: it is entirely expected that estimated effects will change (even dramatically) when these variables are controlled for, and such changes should not be regarded as a sign of instability

title: Exclusion rules that change sample size create precision nonequivalence
guidance: Alternative inclusion or exclusion criteria can produce very different sample sizes across specifications, as in a study whose samples ranged from 114 to 300 or meta-analyses with five to 42 studies. Specifications then differ in power and precision, so their estimates are not equally informative and should not be pooled as if arbitrary.
action: Report the sample size of each specification and treat large swings in sample size as a reason to separate rather than pool specifications.
quote: alternative criteria for the inclusion/exclusion of data points (e.g., removal of outliers) result in substantially different sample sizes across specifications

title: Type E, Type N and Type U decisions
guidance: Type E decisions (principled equivalence) involve alternatives that are truly arbitrary and belong in one homogeneous multiverse. Type N decisions (principled nonequivalence) have an objectively better justified option that should be used alone. Type U decisions (uncertainty) involve alternatives that probably differ but cannot be ranked, and call for separate, deliberately exploratory multiverses.
action: Label every decision node in a field's design space as E, N or U, and build separate multiverses for each branch of a U decision.
quote: Type E decisions imply true arbitrariness and are properly used to populate a homogeneous multiverse.

title: Report the rationale for treating alternatives as equivalent
guidance: Selecting specifications on principle does not undermine transparency provided researchers make transparent not only the decisions considered but also the reasoning used to evaluate them. Researchers may not simply declare alternatives equivalent; each classification needs support from evidence or theory.
action: Require that any multiverse cited for a prediction states, node by node, why alternatives were judged equivalent, and discount multiverses that offer no rationale.
quote: What should be transparent are not just the decisions considered in the analysis, but also the rationale for the evaluation of those decisions.

title: Unprincipled multiverse hid a true effect of 0.20 (median 0.01)
guidance: In a simulation with a true direct effect of 0.20, a mechanically generated multiverse of 1,216 specifications yielded a median effect of 0.01, only 27 percent significant results, and opposite signs at the 1st and 99th percentiles. The principled multiverse under the true causal model instead gave six positive, significant effects between 0.14 and 0.16, showing that a smaller homogeneous multiverse can be far more informative than a large mixed one.
action: Do not equate the size of a multiverse with its credibility; prefer small, homogeneous multiverses whose decision nodes are justified.
quote: Investigators using the mean of the multiverse as a presumably robust estimate would wrongly conclude that the effect of inflammation on depression is about zero.

title: Replication, robustness and reproducibility: three distinct tests
guidance: Nosek and colleagues adopt the National Academies' distinctions: replication tests a prior finding with different data, robustness tests it with the same data and a different analysis strategy, and reproducibility tests it with the same data and the same analysis. A multiverse analysis is therefore a robustness test, not a replication, and the map should label each piece of follow-up evidence by which of the three it provides.
action: Tag every follow-up study on the map as a reproducibility, robustness or replication test according to whether data and analysis were held fixed.
quote: Replication refers to testing the reliability of a prior finding with different data. Robustness refers to testing the reliability of a prior finding using the same data and a different analysis strategy.

title: Process versus outcome reproducibility failures
guidance: A process reproducibility failure occurs when the original analysis cannot be repeated because data, code or software are unavailable; an outcome reproducibility failure occurs when reanalysis of the same data yields a different result. Only the latter suggests the original result is wrong, but both undermine credibility, and Artner and colleagues reproduced just 70 percent of 232 findings.
action: When recording reproducibility evidence, distinguish studies that could not be re-run from studies that were re-run and gave different results.
quote: Whereas an outcome reproducibility failure suggests that the original result may be wrong, a process reproducibility failure merely indicates that the original result cannot be verified.

title: Fragile findings depend on exclusion and covariate decisions
guidance: Robust evidence survives reasonable variations in analysis, while fragile evidence depends on specific decisions such as which observations are excluded and which covariates are included; the 29-team Silberzahn study is cited as showing substantial analyst-induced variation. A fragile finding is not necessarily wrong, but fragility is a risk factor for replicability and, absent a precommitted plan, raises concerns about p-hacking and overfitting.
action: Treat exclusion rules and covariate sets as the first choices to vary when assessing whether a field's findings are robust or fragile.
quote: A fragile finding is not necessarily wrong, but fragility is a risk factor for replicability and generalizability.

title: Replication is a theoretical commitment, not an exact copy
guidance: Because no two studies are identical, the authors define a replication as a study whose innumerable differences from the original are believed to be irrelevant for obtaining evidence about the same finding. This makes the designation theory-dependent: it rests on the field's understanding of which sample, setting, treatment and outcome features matter, which is exactly the set of assumptions an epistemic map should make explicit.
action: For each replication claim, record which differences from the original were assumed irrelevant and whether the field's theory justifies that assumption.
quote: A study is a replication when the innumerable differences from the original study are believed to be irrelevant for obtaining the evidence about the same finding.

title: Generalizability test versus replication: can negatives disconfirm?
guidance: Every replication is a generalizability test, but a generalizability test counts as a replication only if all outcomes, positive and negative, would alter confidence in the original finding. If a negative result would merely be read as a boundary condition, the study is a generalizability test, and the authors note that so-called conceptual replications usually fall in this category because they rarely disconfirm.
action: Classify a follow-up study as a replication only if the field would have accepted a null result as evidence against the original finding.
quote: A generalizability test is a replication only if all outcomes of the test alter our confidence in the original finding

title: No single criterion defines replication success
guidance: The review lists several dichotomous criteria for judging whether the same outcome occurred, such as significance in the same direction, whether one estimate falls in the other's interval, and small-telescopes tests, and notes that each gives some perspective and none is definitive. Meta-analytic approaches that focus on effect sizes and heterogeneity are more mature but are undermined by publication bias and mixing studies of unequal quality.
action: Report replication outcomes on the map using at least two criteria and the effect-size ratio rather than a single pass or fail verdict.
quote: There are a variety of options for a dichotomous assessment of replication outcomes, each of which provides some perspective and none of which is definitive.

title: A finding can replicate and still be invalid
guidance: Reproducibility, robustness and replicability do not guarantee that treatments worked as intended, that measures captured the intended constructs, or that interpretations match the evidence. For a field map this means replication status and validity of operationalisations are separate dimensions, and a robustly replicated effect may still rest on a questionable measurement assumption.
action: Keep construct validity of measures and manipulations as a separate assumption layer on the map, independent of replication evidence.
quote: A finding can be reproducible, robust, replicable, and invalid at the same time.

title: Low power plus 90% positive results implies bias
guidance: Median statistical power in published psychology is often below 0.50, and a meta-analysis of 44 power reviews found mean power of 0.24 for small effects with no improvement since the 1960s, yet 90 percent or more of primary outcomes are reported as significant. The authors argue this disjoint cannot be reconciled without publication bias or questionable practices that inflate effects, a diagnostic that can be applied to any literature.
action: Compare the field's typical power with its share of significant results and flag a large gap as evidence of selective reporting.
quote: The evidence of low power and high positive result rates cannot be reconciled easily without inferring the influence of publication bias

title: Across 307 replications, 64% succeeded at 68% effect size
guidance: Pooling systematic and multi-site replications from the decade (n = 307), 64 percent found statistically significant evidence in the same direction and effect sizes averaged 68 percent of the originals, even though replication samples were on average 15 times larger. The Open Science Collaboration's 36 percent and Camerer's 62 percent are the benchmark figures a management field can compare itself against.
action: Use these benchmark replication rates and effect-size shrinkage when setting prior credibility weights for unreplicated findings.
quote: Considering all replications (n = 307), 64% reported statistically significant evidence in the same direction, with effect sizes 68% as large as in the original studies.

title: Context sensitivity must be demonstrated, not assumed
guidance: Invoking contextual sensitivity to explain a failed replication is common, but the review argues it demands evidence; when examined directly, presumed context sensitivity has often failed to account for replication failures, and heterogeneity across sites is usually modest. Hidden moderators are a consequence of underspecified theories, so the burden is on the field to state auxiliary assumptions about sample, setting and outcome in advance.
action: Record claimed boundary conditions as testable assumptions and downweight post hoc context explanations that lack direct evidence.
quote: invoking it to explain the difference between the results of an original study and a replication demands evidence

title: Surprising results and weak p-values predict replication failure
guidance: Features of original studies predict replicability: studies with more surprising results were less likely to replicate, lower original p-values were associated with success, and in small-sample literatures with publication bias large observed effects can signal overestimation rather than large true effects. These are cheap indicators a reader can apply before any replication exists.
action: Weight a finding's credibility down when it is surprising, barely significant, or shows an implausibly large effect from a small sample.
quote: large observed effects can be a sign of overestimated or false positives rather than of large true effects

title: Report all analytic decisions to expose forking paths
guidance: Low transparency hampers replication because it is hard to know what was done; Errington and colleagues could not build any of 193 replication protocols without asking the original authors. The authors call for transparent reporting of all analytic decisions and outcomes to avoid unacknowledged gardens of forking paths, which is the raw material a multiverse needs.
action: Extract every reported analytic decision from a study and note where the paper is silent, since silence hides forking paths.
quote: This includes transparent reporting of all analytic decisions and outcomes to avoid unacknowledged "gardens of forking paths"

title: Replication outcomes are predictable from study features
guidance: Prediction markets, surveys and structured elicitation correlated with observed replication success at r of 0.52, 0.48 and 0.75, and machine learning models using sample size, p-values, effect sizes and whether effects are interactions performed similarly. Because replicability is predictable, readers can form calibrated credibility judgements from study features before replications exist.
action: Use sample size, p-value, effect size and main-versus-interaction status as inputs to the credibility weight of each mapped finding.
quote: statistical properties like the sample sizes, p-values, and effect sizes of the original studies, as well as whether the effects are main effects or interaction effects, are predictive of successful replication

title: Improve replicability through more severe tests
guidance: Replicability improves by conducting more severe tests: more observations, stronger measures and manipulations, stricter inference criteria, preregistration to guard against p-hacking and HARKing, and taking alternative explanations seriously through robustness checks, cross-validation and internal replications. Conclusions should be calibrated to how much the inference could have been shaped by prior observation of the data.
action: Score each mapped study on test severity, including whether robustness checks and stated constraints on generality accompany the main result.
quote: taking alternative explanations seriously by undertaking robustness checks, cross-validation, and internal replications

title: Metascience documents threats to efficient knowledge accumulation
guidance: The manifesto opens by listing the conditions that raise the probability that a published finding is incorrect: low sample size, small effects, data dredging, conflicts of interest and competitive siloed work. It notes that metascience has produced substantial empirical evidence for the prevalence of these threats, so a field map should treat them as documented risks rather than hypothetical ones.
action: Record, for each mapped literature, the typical sample sizes and effect sizes and whether data dredging or conflicts of interest are plausible threats.
quote: Low sample size, small effect sizes, data dredging (also known as P-hacking), conflicts of interest

title: Thousands of reasonable pipelines make false positives likely
guidance: The authors note that in a high-dimensional dataset there may be hundreds or thousands of reasonable alternative approaches to analysing the same data, citing Carp's finding of almost as many unique analytical pipelines as fMRI studies and that nearly 7,000 pipelines made over 90 percent of brain voxels significant in at least one analysis. The lesson for management research is that a single reported specification carries little information when the space of defensible alternatives is large.
action: Enumerate the defensible alternative pipelines for a field's standard design before judging how informative any single published result is.
quote: there may be hundreds or thousands of reasonable alternative approaches to analysing the same data

title: Confirmation and hindsight bias disguise P-hacking as discovery
guidance: During analysis, confirmation and hindsight biases make researchers accept outcomes that fit expectations and dismiss others as products of suboptimal design, so hypotheses that emerge from the data get reported without acknowledging their post hoc origin. The manifesto calls this self-deception rather than discovery and warns it can dramatically increase the false discovery rate.
action: When reading a paper, check whether the stated hypothesis could have been formed after seeing the results and flag such cases as exploratory.
quote: Hypotheses may emerge that fit the data and are then reported without indication or recognition of their post hoc origin

title: Preregistration is a form of blinding the analyst
guidance: Blinding is presented as the most effective protection against self-deception, and preregistration of the design, primary outcomes and analysis plan is described as a highly effective form of blinding because the data do not yet exist and the outcomes are unknown. For a field map, a preregistered analysis plan is therefore evidence that analytic choices were not data-contingent.
action: Treat a preregistered analysis plan as the strongest available signal that a study's specification was chosen independently of its data.
quote: is a highly effective form of blinding because the data do not exist and the outcomes are not yet known

title: Statistical power is persistently below fifty percent
guidance: Studies of statistical power across time and disciplines persistently find it below, sometimes well below, fifty percent, and low power raises both false-positive and false-negative rates, so it offers no advantage for accumulating knowledge. The manifesto attributes its persistence to incentives, misunderstanding and lack of resources, and proposes team science and multi-site designs as a remedy.
action: Record the typical sample size and implied power of a field's standard design and treat chronically low power as a reason to discount surprising significant results.
quote: Studies of statistical power persistently find it to be below (sometimes well below) 50%, across both time and the different disciplines studied

title: Many Labs: one protocol across dozens of laboratories
guidance: The Many Labs projects are offered as the model for distributed collaboration in the social and behavioural sciences: dozens of laboratories run the same protocol to obtain precise effect-size estimates and to evaluate variability across samples and settings. This separates true heterogeneity across contexts from noise, which is what a map of a field's generalisation claims needs.
action: Where a prediction has been tested only in single-site studies, note that cross-site variability in the effect is unknown.
quote: with dozens of laboratories implementing the same research protocol to obtain highly precise estimates of effect sizes, and evaluate variability across samples and settings

title: P-hacking is any data-contingent analysis decision
guidance: The manifesto defines P-hacking broadly as practices that inflate spurious findings when analysis decisions, such as the selection of models, exclusion rules and covariates, are made with knowledge of the observed data. Outcome switching is the clinical example, but the definition covers the control-variable and sample-restriction choices common in management research.
action: List the model, exclusion and covariate choices in a field's standard design and ask whether each could have been made after seeing the data.
quote: when analysis decisions are made with knowledge of the observed data, such as selection of models, exclusion rules and covariates

title: Strongest preregistration: register plus prespecify design and analysis
guidance: The strongest form of preregistration combines registering the study with a commitment to publish and closely prespecifying the design, primary outcome and analysis plan before the data are known. This addresses publication bias by making all research discoverable and addresses P-hacking by keeping analytic decisions data-independent, and it makes explicit the line between confirmatory and exploratory work.
action: Classify each mapped study as confirmatory only if its design, outcome and analysis plan were prespecified before the data were known.
quote: The strongest form of pre-registration involves both registering the study (with a commitment to make the results public) and closely pre-specifying the study design, primary outcome and analysis plan

title: Only 13% of preregistered trials reported outcomes as registered
guidance: Even with mandatory preregistration, one study found that just 13 percent of clinical trials published outcomes fully consistent with their registered commitments, and in psychology about 70 percent of published reports omitted at least one outcome measure, with omitted measures more likely to be null and smaller. Registration therefore does not guarantee faithful reporting, and deviations should be checked rather than assumed absent.
action: When a study is preregistered, compare the published outcomes and conditions with the registration before crediting it as confirmatory.
quote: one study observed that just 13% of trials published outcomes completely consistent with the pre-registered commitments

title: Transparency is superior to trust
guidance: The manifesto argues that claims become credible through community review, critique, extension and reproduction of the supporting evidence; without transparency, credibility rests only on trust in the authority of the originator. For a reader of a field's literature this means that the weight placed on a result should depend on whether its methodology, data and analysis process are inspectable.
action: Give more credibility weight to results whose data, code and workflow are open than to results that must be taken on the authors' word.
quote: without transparency, claims only achieve credibility based on trust in the confidence or authority of the originator. Transparency is superior to trust.

title: Full disclosure: readers cannot evaluate undisclosed measurement choices
guidance: Box 6 explains that the informational value of a significant dependent variable depends on how many variables were collected: one of fifteen variables will reach P below 0.05 by chance 54 percent of the time. Authors who do not disclose how many measures, exclusions and manipulations they used leave readers unable to evaluate the research; the 21-word disclosure statement is the minimal remedy.
action: Check whether mapped studies disclose sample-size determination, all exclusions, all manipulations and all measures, and flag those that do not.
quote: if authors do not tell us whether they collected one or fifteen variables readers cannot evaluate their research

title: Replication alone may not remove false results
guidance: In its conclusion the manifesto cautions that proposed solutions create their own challenges: it is unclear which studies deserve replication and what replication strategies are efficient, and a simulation suggests that replication alone may not suffice to rid the literature of false results. A field map should therefore combine replication evidence with design scrutiny and transparency indicators rather than relying on replication counts.
action: Do not treat a replication count as sufficient evidence of credibility; combine it with assessments of design validity and reporting transparency.
quote: a recent simulation suggests that replication alone may not suffice to rid us of false results

title: Widely used methods can turn out to be invalid
guidance: The authors note that metascience questions what was previously taken for granted, including widely used statistical methods, citing the finding that the most popular fMRI spatial extent software produced unacceptably high false-positive rates. Standard methods in a management field are assumptions too, and their validity should be recorded rather than presumed.
action: List the default statistical procedures of the field as explicit assumptions on the map and note any metascience evidence about their error rates.
quote: What was previously taken for granted may be questioned, such as widely used statistical methods

title: Meta-research is the study of research itself
guidance: Ioannidis defines meta-research as the study of research methods, reporting, reproducibility, evaluation and incentives. Mapping a management field's predictions, designs and assumptions is itself a meta-research activity, and the paper frames it as a way to make the research enterprise more credible and useful.
action: Frame the field map as a meta-research product that documents methods and reporting, not only results.
quote: Meta-research is the study of research itself: its methods, reporting, reproducibility, evaluation, and incentives.

title: Science can evaluate its own methods and incentives
guidance: The paper's central claim is that science can turn its tools on itself to assess methods, reporting, reproducibility, evaluation and incentives. The objective is to understand and improve how research is performed, communicated, verified, evaluated and rewarded, which is exactly the frame under which design assumptions in a field should be audited.
action: Treat the assumptions behind a field's standard designs as objects of empirical study rather than as settled conventions.
quote: The objective is to understand and improve how we perform, communicate, verify, evaluate, and reward research

title: Twenty binary choices give over a million analyses
guidance: Ioannidis illustrates the scale of analytic flexibility: with only twenty binary design or analysis choices there are 1,048,576 ways to analyse the same data, so almost any result is attainable unless methods and analysis standards are safeguarded. This is the quantitative core of why a multiverse or specification map is needed to interpret a field's reported findings.
action: Count the discretionary binary choices in a field's standard design and use that count to motivate which ones to vary in a multiverse.
quote: With increasing research complexity, multifarious choices emerge on how to design studies and analyze data.

title: Data sharing and preregistration remain uncommon
guidance: The paper reports that generated research data are massive but fragmented and often nontransparent, and that full data sharing and preregistration of protocols are still uncommon in most fields. For a field map this means the absence of shared data and preregistered protocols should be recorded as a credibility limitation, not as the neutral default.
action: Record for each mapped study whether data, code and a preregistered protocol are available, and downweight credibility when they are not.
quote: Full data sharing and preregistration of protocols are still uncommon in most fields

title: Questionable research practices are used by most scientists
guidance: Citing survey evidence, Ioannidis notes that questionable research practices are used by most scientists, not as fraud but as cutting corners to obtain more interesting-looking results. He adds that understanding the boundary between bias and legitimate creative exploration is itself an open question, which is the boundary a multiverse analysis tries to make explicit.
action: Assume that undisclosed analytic flexibility is the norm in a literature and plan the multiverse to make the plausible corner-cutting choices visible.
quote: not fraud (which is rare) but "cutting corners" to achieve more interesting-looking results

title: Reproduction attempts show high rates of nonreproducibility
guidance: The paper summarises that efforts to reproduce high-profile studies have found high rates of nonreproducibility, that most scientists agree a reproducibility crisis exists, and that meta-analyses face their own biases. A field map should therefore not treat a published or even meta-analysed effect as settled without replication evidence.
action: Attach replication status to each prediction on the map and flag effects supported only by original studies or by meta-analyses of them.
quote: Efforts to reproduce high-profile studies have shown high rates of nonreproducibility

title: Research standards and threats differ across fields
guidance: Ioannidis stresses that disciplines differ in research standards and challenges, and that new fields continuously emerge with different norms. Methodological guidance imported from one field, such as psychology or biomedicine, must therefore be checked against the designs, tools and biases actually prevalent in the management field being mapped.
action: Profile the field's own typical designs and biases before applying replication or reporting benchmarks borrowed from another discipline.
quote: Different disciplines may differ in research standards and challenges (Box 1).

title: Box 1: features of research practice to profile per field
guidance: Box 1 lists the dimensions along which fields vary and which a field profile should cover: the types of study designs, measurement tools and statistical methods commonly used or misused, the common biases and whether they are easy to fix, and the prevalence of questionable practices. These headings double as a checklist for the legend of an epistemic map.
action: Use the Box 1 headings on designs, tools, methods and biases as the top-level categories when profiling a field.
quote: Types of study designs commonly used or misused

title: Box 1: effect sizes, heterogeneity and share of true results
guidance: Among the field features that vary, Box 1 includes the distribution of observed effect sizes, the typical heterogeneity of results across studies, and the proportion of results that are true, exaggerated or entirely false. These are the quantities a multiverse or many-analysts study estimates for a given prediction, so they belong on the map as credibility weights.
action: For each prediction, record typical effect size, cross-study heterogeneity and any estimate of the share of exaggerated or false results.
quote: Proportion of results that are true, exaggerated, or entirely false

title: Box 1: replication and transparency standards of a field
guidance: Box 1 closes with the replication and transparency standards that characterise a field: enforcement of preregistration, use of replication studies, exact replication versus corroboration or triangulation, sharing of raw and processed data, and sharing of software and code. A field map should score the field on each of these so that readers know how much reported results can be trusted.
action: Score the mapped field on preregistration, replication use, data sharing and code sharing, and show those scores in the map legend.
quote: Extent of use of exact replication versus corroboration or triangulation

title: Reproducibility uses the same data; replicability uses new data
guidance: The framework defines reproducibility as testing whether an original study's results can be reproduced with the same data, and replicability as testing whether they hold in new data, then splits these into computational, recreate and robustness reproducibility and direct and conceptual replicability. The vocabulary is chosen to match emerging standard usage in the social sciences.
action: Adopt this five-type vocabulary when labelling every reproduction or replication on the map so that rates are not compared across incommensurable types.
quote: Reproducibility is defined as testing if the results of an original study can be reproduced using the same data and replicability is defined as testing if the results of an original study hold in new data

title: About 70 percent of robustness tests held, with t-values 20 percent lower
guidance: The Institute for Replication's robustness reproducibility tests of 110 economics and political science papers found roughly 70 percent of tests significant and average t or z values about 20 percent lower than the originals. This is the broadest available estimate of how published estimates fare under alternative reasonable specifications.
action: Use a prior that a published observational estimate survives independent robustness checks about two times in three, with a somewhat smaller test statistic.
quote: about 70% of the robustness tests were statistically significant and on average the t/z‐values were about 20% lower in the robustness tests

title: Only 47 percent of AER observational findings were robust
guidance: Campbell and colleagues tested 17 systematically selected observational papers from the American Economic Review; all main findings were originally significant, but only 47 percent of robustness tests were significant and test statistics were about 40 percent lower, which the authors read as evidence of substantial credibility problems and selective reporting.
action: Treat top-journal observational results as no more than even odds to survive robustness reproducibility until checked.
quote: only 47% of the robustness tests were statistically significant and the t/z‐values in the robustness tests were about 40% lower than in the original results

title: Different reproducibility types are not comparable
guidance: A typology prevents comparing apples and oranges: computational reproducibility should not be expected to equal robustness reproducibility, nor robustness reproducibility to equal direct replicability. Terminology is a coordination problem, and failure to coordinate produces confusion and incorrect inferences across studies.
action: Never pool or compare reproducibility rates on the map without first checking that they belong to the same type.
quote: there is for instance no reason to expect computational reproducibility to be the same as robustness reproducibility or robustness reproducibility to be the same as direct replicability

title: Early computational reproducibility in economics was 4 to 22 percent
guidance: Dewald and colleagues sought code and data for 54 macroeconomics papers and reproduced only two, or 22 percent of the nine for which materials were available; later studies covering over 500 papers also report meagre rates. Computational reproducibility, which should be trivially high, is not.
action: Record whether a focal study has passed a data-editor or independent computational reproducibility check before weighting its estimate.
quote: only managed to reproduce the results of two (4%) papers

title: Recreate reproducibility: reanalysis without code or exact data
guidance: Recreate reproducibility means reanalysing an original study as closely as possible from the information in the paper when the analysis code, the exact dataset, or both are unavailable; its hardest sub-type requires recreating both. Systematic studies of this type in finance and management report low success rates.
action: When a reproduction had to rebuild sample or code from the paper, label it recreate reproducibility and note which of code or data was missing.
quote: Recreate reproducibility implies trying to reanalyze the results of an original study as closely as possible without having access to the analysis code and/or the exact data the code was applied to

title: Robustness reproducibility ranges from a few checks to a full multiverse
guidance: Testing a hypothesis involves many analytical decisions, and a paper reports one combination plus some robustness tests; robustness reproducibility re-tests on the same data across alternative reasonable decisions, from a handful to a complete multiverse or specification curve, which the authors see as the ideal.
action: Record how much of the reasonable specification space a robustness check covered, and treat a full multiverse as the reference standard.
quote: anything from testing a few alternative analytical decisions to a full‐blown multiverse or specification curve analysis that explores all combinations of reasonable analytical decisions

title: Published comments are selected on non-robustness
guidance: Many individual robustness studies in economics appear as journal comments, but general conclusions cannot be drawn from them because they are likely selected on the result being non-robust. Systematic studies with pre-specified paper selection are needed for unbiased rates.
action: Do not infer a field-level robustness rate from comments and critiques; use only systematically sampled reproducibility studies for base rates.
quote: It is however difficult to draw general conclusions about robustness reproducibility from such studies as they are likely to be selected based on results being non‐robust

title: Robust on the same data can still fail in new data
guidance: Robustness reproducibility rates and replication rates measure different things, so they cannot be compared directly: a result may survive every reasonable alternative specification on the original data and still fail to replicate in a new sample.
action: Keep specification robustness and new-data replication as separate credibility dimensions on the map rather than collapsing them into one score.
quote: a result can for instance be robust in a test of robustness reproducibility but still fail to replicate

title: Direct replications by population: same, similar, different
guidance: Because samples can rarely be drawn from exactly the same population at the same time, the authors recommend keeping the term direct replication whenever design and analysis are unchanged, while recording whether the sample comes from the same, a similar, or a different population; the same scheme applies to observational data.
action: Tag every replication with the population relation to the original, since a failure in a different population is weaker evidence against the original.
quote: we distinguish between three possible types of direct replications: direct replications based on samples from the same population, direct replications based on samples from similar populations

title: Relative effect size is the key indicator of systematic bias
guidance: The relative effect size indicator divides the average effect size across reproducibility tests by the original effect size; values below one indicate systematic overestimation in the original. The authors regard it as the most important reproducibility indicator because it measures bias directly rather than crossing a significance threshold.
action: Report the ratio of re-estimated to original effect sizes for each finding on the map, not just whether significance was retained.
quote: In our view the relative effect size indicator is the most important indicator of reproducibility as it directly measures systematic bias in original studies

title: Variation indicator: spread across specifications relative to the original standard error
guidance: For robustness reproducibility the authors add a variation indicator: the standard deviation of effect sizes across all robustness tests, including the original if reasonable, divided by the original standard error. A value of one means specification variation equals sampling variation; higher values mean lower robustness, even when average effects and significance look fine.
action: Compute specification spread in units of the original standard error when summarising a multiverse, and flag values at or above one.
quote: It is defined as the standard deviation in effect sizes among all the robustness tests divided by the standard error of the original effect size

title: Power replications at 90 percent for half the original effect
guidance: Because the sample size of a replication usually differs from the original and true effects are likely overestimated in original studies, underpowered replications produce false negatives on the significance indicator; the authors recommend at least 90 percent power to detect 50 percent of the original effect size.
action: Before counting a non-significant replication as evidence against a finding, check that it had roughly 90 percent power for half the original effect.
quote: We recommend ideally having at least 90% power to detect 50% of the original effect size

title: Scholars disagree about which specifications are reasonable
guidance: Ideally all reasonable analysis paths would enter a multiverse, but there is no clear way to determine them and scholars disagree about what is reasonable, as reproducibility debates in journal comments and the wide variation in choices across multi-analyst studies both show. Identifying reasonable paths, possibly by crowdsourcing, is an open problem.
action: Document the inclusion rule for specifications in any multiverse on the map and note contested choices as assumptions rather than settled facts.
quote: it is not clear how to determine these analysis paths and different scholars can disagree about which specifications are reasonable

title: Endogeneity: predictor correlated with the residual, bias unpredictable
guidance: Hill and colleagues define endogeneity formally as a predictor correlating with the unexplained residual of the outcome, and stress that the resulting bias cannot be predicted by methods alone and is as likely to overestimate as underestimate the coefficient. This makes endogeneity a threat to the sign and size of every non-experimental estimate on a field map, not merely a source of inflation.
action: Record for each non-experimental finding that its direction and magnitude are uncertain under endogeneity, rather than assuming the bias only inflates the effect.
quote: the bias cannot be predicted with methods alone and the coefficients are just as likely to be overestimated as underestimated

title: Misapplied endogeneity cures spread through the literature
guidance: Using a disease metaphor, the authors note that methodologists have repeatedly found remedies for endogeneity administered incorrectly, so papers thought to be cured are not, and later studies that imitate them accumulate biased findings and propagate the incorrect practice. For a field map this means the prevalence of a technique is no evidence of its validity in that literature.
action: Do not infer that a design assumption is reasonable because many papers in the field share it; check whether the practice traces to a methodological source or to imitation.
quote: resulting not only in the accumulation of biased findings but also in the spread of the incorrect practice

title: Understanding the residual is a theoretical exercise
guidance: Because the residual contains everything not captured by the predictors, deciding whether x is related to it cannot be settled by statistics alone; the authors require that any diagnosis of endogeneity and any remedy be accompanied by a theoretical rationale about which variables or events would link x to the residual. Design assumptions are therefore substantive claims about the world that a map can state and evaluate.
action: For each design, write out the theoretical argument for why the key predictor is unrelated to the residual, and treat the absence of such an argument as a gap.
quote: defining the source of endogeneity and determining an appropriate remedy must always be accompanied by a theoretical rationale of variables or events that would cause x to be related to u

title: Four causes: omitted variable, simultaneity, measurement error, selection
guidance: Following Wooldridge, the paper separates endogeneity into four causes that bias results differently: omitted variables related to both x and y, simultaneity where y also affects x, measurement error in x correlated with y, and selection, which splits into non-random selection into the sample and non-random selection of treatment. Each cause needs its own diagnosis and remedy, so a map should classify threats by cause rather than by the generic label.
action: Classify each identification threat on the map under one of the four causes and note that a remedy for one cause does not address the others.
quote: The final cause of endogeneity is selection, which is divided into two subtypes. Bias can arise if selection into a sample is not random

title: Only 1.5% of 435 papers report endogeneity changing results
guidance: Of 435 top-journal management articles mentioning endogeneity, 58 percent addressed it in the main analysis and 30 percent through robustness tests, but only two articles (1.5 percent) reported that results differed after accounting for it. The authors read this as a sign that published papers present endogeneity as addressed and harmless, which is implausible given how often methods are misapplied.
action: Treat a literature in which endogeneity corrections never change conclusions as a warning sign of selective reporting rather than as reassurance.
quote: only 1.5% (k = 2) of the articles offer evidence the results differ from the primary analysis after addressing endogeneity

title: The endogeneity equivalent of p-hacking
guidance: Because vague explanations of instruments and techniques prevent readers from assessing claims, the authors warn of two consequences: a rose-tinted literature where only unaffected results are published, and weak tests chosen for their tendency to leave results unchanged, which they call the endogeneity equivalent of p-hacking. The choice of correction method is thus itself a researcher degree of freedom.
action: Include the choice of endogeneity correction (instrument set, estimator, selection model) among the specification choices varied in a multiverse.
quote: statistical techniques are applied not based on their appropriateness or quality but on their proclivity to leave results unchanged

title: Proxies and poorly measured controls can create new bias
guidance: A control removes omitted variable bias only if it measures the omitted variable well; otherwise it acts as a proxy with measurement error, and plugging in a proxy must not itself create a residual-predictor correlation. The authors cite evidence that poorly measured controls are hazardous and that arbitrarily adding extra controls can also bias estimates, and they discuss the impact threshold of a confounding variable as a more principled way to judge how strong an omitted variable would need to be.
action: Record how well each control variable measures the confounder it stands for, and use sensitivity bounds rather than control counts to judge omitted-variable risk.
quote: Pei, Pischke, and Schwandt (2019) note the hazards of poorly measured control variables, while Spector and Brannick (2011) discuss how arbitrarily including extra controls can also create bias.

title: Report instrument relevance, first stage and tests
guidance: Whatever estimator is used, two-stage least squares, generalized method of moments or structural equation modelling, the authors stress that the cause of endogeneity must be identified and the instrument justified, that the assumptions built into the approach must be stated explicitly, and that studies should show first-stage analyses and relevant tests. In their sample 71 percent of instrumental-variable papers explained their instruments but many explanations were too vague to assess.
action: For each instrumental-variable study, check that the first-stage results, the rationale for the exclusion restriction and the specification tests are reported.
quote: Studies should explain the relevance of the instrumental variable(s) and estimation technique, show "first-stage" or similar analyses, and provide relevant tests for any approach used

title: Simultaneity cannot be fixed with control variables
guidance: When the outcome also affects the predictor, no control variable can be added to repair the estimate, so control and proxy solutions are inapplicable and instrumental variables or exogenous shocks are needed. The authors also note that lagging variables only helps under conditions on the residual, so temporal separation does not automatically solve reverse causality.
action: When a prediction plausibly runs in both directions, mark designs that rely on controls or simple lags as not having addressed simultaneity.
quote: with simultaneity between a predictor x and outcome y, there are no controls that can be added to the model to fix the problem

title: Treatment-effect methods assume, rather than fix, no endogeneity
guidance: Difference-in-differences and matching or synthetic control approaches estimate average treatment effects but, in general, do not address endogeneity; they rest on ignorability or selection-on-observables assumptions that unmeasured variables affect treated and untreated groups equally. They solve important problems but are not catch-all cures and require their own theoretical and empirical justification.
action: For every difference-in-differences or matching study, state the selection-on-observables or parallel-trends assumption explicitly as an untested premise on the map.
quote: the claim of unbiased estimates rests on the assumption that unmeasured variables affect all sampled groups equally

title: Regression discontinuity approximates randomisation near the threshold
guidance: A regression discontinuity design exploits an arbitrary cutoff so that observations just below and just above the threshold should be approximately equal on all omitted variables, allowing a comparison like a true experiment. The authors note the open choices this creates: how wide a bandwidth around the threshold to use and whether treated and untreated units contaminate each other.
action: When mapping a regression discontinuity study, record the bandwidth choice and contamination checks as analytic decisions to vary in robustness analysis.
quote: The observations just below and just above the threshold should be approximately equal on all omitted variables (similar to random assignment)

title: State the specific cause, not that endogeneity was addressed
guidance: The first recommendation is a clear diagnosis: any endogeneity concern should be stated in terms of a specific cause, omitted variable, simultaneity, measurement error, selection into sample or selection of treatment, with as much theoretical rationale as possible, replacing generic statements that endogeneity was addressed. Reviewers' critiques should likewise name a specific cause rather than invoking endogeneity as a boogieman.
action: When extracting assumptions from a paper, translate every generic endogeneity claim into the specific cause it refers to, or record that the cause was unspecified.
quote: comments akin to "we addressed endogeneity" should be replaced by the specific cause (e.g., simultaneity) of endogeneity and rationale for why that cause may be present

title: Justify the remedy and report naive results alongside corrected ones
guidance: The second recommendation requires justifying that the problem exists, justifying the technique from methodological sources rather than by citing a precedent paper, stating the technique's assumptions explicitly, and reporting enough detail, including the uncorrected results, first-stage models and specification tests, for readers to judge whether the method was needed and adequate.
action: Check that naive and corrected estimates are both reported and that the remedy is justified from methodological literature rather than by precedent.
quote: the naïve results—without any correction—should be presented alongside the results from the approach that attempted to address the specific form of endogeneity

title: No single study can mitigate all endogeneity concerns
guidance: The final recommendation is that authors and gatekeepers accept that no one study can fully mitigate every endogeneity concern; confidence that a specific threat is addressed comes only from repeated studies of the same question with different designs and analyses, and even experiments require triangulation across designs, samples and operationalisations. A field map should therefore track which threats have been addressed across the body of studies rather than within each one.
action: Aggregate across the field's studies to show which endogeneity causes have been addressed by at least one credible design and which remain untested.
quote: Only through repeated studies of a research question using different designs and analyses can we gain confidence that a specific endogeneity threat is fully addressed.

title: Reproduction, time generalization and far replication
guidance: The empirical review applies three replication types to each study: a reproduction that strictly follows the original data, sample, measurement and specification; a time generalization that samples the same source in other periods with all else unchanged; and a far replication that swaps in alternative data sources for key variables. Each isolates a different assumption of the original design.
action: When documenting re-examinations of a finding, label each as reproduction, time generalization or far replication so that what was held constant is explicit.
quote: The first is a reproduction, in which we strictly follow the methodology of the original paper including the data, sample, measurement, and specifications.

title: Secondary data create discordance between concept and measure
guidance: Corruption studies rely on reputable secondary sources, but recent reviews consistently flag that this creates discordance between theoretical concepts and empirical measures. The authors observe that country-level measures are frequently used to test theories stated at the firm level.
action: For every construct, record the level at which the theory operates and the level at which the proxy is measured, and flag mismatches as questionable assumptions.
quote: scholars use secondary data from reputable sources, but the use of secondary data creates corresponding concerns about discordances between theoretical concepts and empirical measures

title: Firm-level mechanisms tested with country-level variables lack reliability
guidance: The authors argue that conclusions in corruption research may lack reliability because theorizing about firm-level mechanisms, nuanced conceptualization of the corruption type, and corresponding measurement acuity are rarely implemented together. Theory about managerial capabilities is frequently tested with aggregate country indices that cannot speak to the mechanism.
action: When a prediction is about a firm-level mechanism, check whether any variable in the design varies at the firm level; if not, mark the mechanism as untested.
quote: We often observe that studies theorize on mechanisms at the firm level while testing hypotheses at the country level

title: A composite perception index is a noisy proxy for business corruption
guidance: The Corruption Perception Index captures the scale and pervasiveness of corruption and includes household survey respondents, so only part of its empirical domain concerns the business-level corruption that the theory is about. Even with clearer concepts, a measure whose attributes do not align with the conception leaves the mechanism untested.
action: When a design uses a composite index as the key independent variable, document which dimensions of the construct the index actually covers and which it does not.
quote: the measure has noise: only part of its empirical domain relates to the pervasiveness of business level corruption

title: LeBel's four replication types: data crossed with analysis
guidance: Following LeBel and colleagues, the review distinguishes analytical reproducibility (same data, same analyses), analytical robustness (same data, different analyses), effect replicability (different data, same analyses) and effect generalization (different data, different analyses). The authors begin each case with reproducibility, then test effect replicability in a new period, then analytical robustness with alternative operationalizations.
action: Place each re-examination of a finding in the two-by-two of data and analysis, and sequence new checks from reproducibility outward.
quote: (1) analytical reproducibility (same data, same analyses); (2) analytical robustness (same data, different analyses); (3) effect replicability (different data, same analyses) and (4) effect generalization (different data, different analyses)

title: Independent double coding of reproductions with reconciliation
guidance: Two co-authors reproduced each paper independently, then cross-checked code and reconciled inconsistencies over sample construction, variable coding and specifications; unresolved disagreements went to the full team, independent econometricians, or data providers. Only tests completed after agreement were reported, with all challenges documented.
action: For any reproduction feeding the map, require two independent implementations and a written log of every reconciled discrepancy.
quote: two of the co-authors reproduced each paper independently. After they finished the independent reproductions, they cross-checked each other’s codes and recorded and reconciled inconsistencies

title: Undisclosed sample construction blocks reproduction
guidance: The original study mentioned 89 host countries without listing them, so the reproduction team tried country lists from related databases and could not match the sample size. Sample construction choices that are not reported become unverifiable assumptions of the published estimate.
action: Record the exact sample inclusion rule for each design; where the paper does not state it, mark sample construction as an undisclosed assumption.
quote: The challenge of replicating H&Z is incomplete disclosure regarding sample construction

title: Small samples with many correlated regressors give unstable estimates
guidance: The authors attribute non-replication of one study partly to its specification: a small-N sample with many independent variables, including a large control set with moderate to high correlations, is prone to Type 1 errors and unstable coefficients. Re-estimating with only the two variables that had found support still returned non-support.
action: Record the ratio of regressors to observations and the correlations among key regressors, and treat specifications that are demanding relative to the sample as low-credibility.
quote: independent variables with moderate to high correlations between independent variables will subject the regressions to Type 1 errors and instability in coefficient estimates

title: Principal components could not separate grand from petty corruption
guidance: Reproducing the factor analysis behind a two-type corruption measure, the authors found that the five indicators had a single eigenvalue above one, that indicators supposed to load on separate factors loaded together, and that Cronbach's alpha was 0.94, implying a one-factor solution. The conceptual distinction had no empirical counterpart in the data used to test it.
action: When a design splits a construct into subtypes via factor analysis, check the eigenvalues and loadings before accepting the subtypes as distinct measured variables.
quote: Hence, we have little evidence that we can empirically differentiate grand corruption from petty corruption using PCA

title: Grand versus petty corruption effects were weakly replicable
guidance: Across a close reproduction, temporal generalization and far replications, the entry-mode effects of grand and petty corruption did not replicate well; a single corruption component showed no effect on entry or partnering strategy. The authors trace the weak replicability to sample reconstruction difficulties and the measurement problem rather than to execution errors.
action: Downweight predictions whose support rests on a measurement distinction that failed to reproduce, and record which replication types were attempted.
quote: The results do not replicate well either in the close reproduction or in the temporal generalization

title: Interaction terms plus misaligned measures amplify instability
guidance: Multicollinearity between an interaction term and its components leads to Type 1 errors and unstable estimates, and the problem worsens when the measure's empirical domain does not match the construct's conceptual domain; small changes in sample size then produce large swings in effect sizes and standard errors.
action: For moderation hypotheses, vary sample composition and centring in the multiverse and check whether the interaction survives, especially when the moderator is a coarse proxy.
quote: Multicollinearity problems between the interaction term and the independent terms, lead to Type 1 errors and unstable estimates

title: Replication success tracked the content validity of the measure
