guidance: The corruption measures used across the four studies varied widely in empirical meaning and often had poor content validity; where content validity was highest, in the baseline corruption-to-investment hypothesis, replications performed well. The authors conclude that misalignment between measurement and conceptualization contributes directly to non-replicability.
action: Score each key measure for content validity relative to the construct and use that score as a credibility weight on the evidence for the prediction.
quote: a lack of alignment between measurement and conceptualization contributes to the lack of replicability

title: Unstated empirical steps confuse those who build on a study
guidance: The replication reports confirm earlier concerns about transparency: the challenges arose from incomplete reporting of empirical steps, which, when left unstated, yield confusion for researchers trying to build on existing work. Greater transparency in reporting is one of the paper's three closing recommendations.
action: Treat each unreported step in sample construction, variable coding or specification as a hidden assumption of the design and list it on the map.
quote: We faced challenges in the replications arose from an incomplete reporting of empirical steps, which, if left unstated, yield confusion for researchers working to build on existing studies.

title: None of four influential corruption studies fully replicated
guidance: The empirical review could not fully replicate any of the four studies with consistency across strict reproductions and generalization tests. The authors conclude that the field must harmonize firm-level theorizing with firm-level modelling, clarify the scale-versus-predictability nature of corruption being studied, and develop acute measures of corruption types.
action: Mark the core country-level corruption-investment relationship as better supported than firm-capability and corruption-type claims, which rest on weaker replicated evidence.
quote: we could not fully replicate the findings of any of these four studies with consistency in strict reproductions and in generalization tests

title: Two-way fixed effects regressions can give wrong-sign estimates
guidance: For years applied researchers estimated complex difference-in-differences designs with unit and time fixed effects regressions, inheriting the causal interpretation that only holds in the two-group, two-period case. Recent work shows that with staggered timing and heterogeneous effects these regressions can produce estimates that are misleading in magnitude and even sign, so many published results are probably wrong in concrete cases.
action: Flag every difference-in-differences study in the mapped field that relies on a single two-way fixed effects coefficient with staggered treatment as needing re-examination with heterogeneity-robust estimators.
quote: simple regressions can fail to estimate meaningful causal parameters when DiD designs are complex and treatment effects vary, producing estimates that are not only misleading in their magnitudes but potentially of the wrong sign

title: No anticipation: treatment has no effect before it begins
guidance: Difference-in-differences requires that treated units' outcomes before treatment equal their untreated potential outcomes, which rules out behavioural responses to an announced but not yet implemented treatment. If anticipation occurs, the effective treatment date is the announcement, and pretreatment comparisons no longer reveal untreated outcome gaps.
action: For each mapped study, check whether treatment could have been anticipated and whether the authors date treatment at announcement or implementation.
quote: if the announcement of Medicaid expansion affected mortality before its actual expansion, "treatment" would begin when the policy was announced rather than implemented

title: Weighting changes the target parameter, not just precision
guidance: With heterogeneous treatment effects, a population-weighted and an unweighted difference-in-differences answer different questions (the effect among counties versus the effect among people). Weights chosen to improve precision also change the estimand, so comparing weighted and unweighted estimates is not a robustness check but a comparison of different parameters.
action: Treat the weighting choice in a difference-in-differences study as a definitional choice about the target population, and in a multiverse interpret weighted versus unweighted results as different estimands rather than as a specification test.
quote: Comparing weighted and unweighted estimates, therefore, does not show whether weighting matters for estimation or inference; these reflect different target parameters.

title: Parallel trends is a restriction on untreated potential outcomes, not randomness
guidance: Unlike randomised trials or instrumental variables, where identification follows statistically from external randomness, parallel trends simply asserts that untreated outcomes would have evolved the same way in treated and comparison groups. Because treatment adoption is usually chosen by actors inside the model, parallel trends need not hold, which is why evaluating it deserves so much attention.
action: Map parallel trends as a substantive behavioural assumption about selection into treatment, and ask what the paper says about why adopters and non-adopters would have trended alike.
quote: parallel trends is just a restriction on untreated potential outcome trends. It does not necessarily come from exogenous variation "outside the model."

title: Selection on time-varying shocks undermines parallel trends
guidance: Parallel trends can hold when selection into treatment depends on permanent differences (fixed effects) that cancel in differences, but if decision-makers respond to recent transitory shocks to the outcome, parallel trends requires much stronger time-series restrictions. There is a trade-off between what agents know when they choose treatment and the dynamics of untreated outcomes.
action: Judge the plausibility of parallel trends by asking whether treatment adopters could have been responding to recent outcome fluctuations rather than to stable characteristics.
quote: in realistic scenarios, parallel trends only holds if some restrictions on the way untreated outcomes enter the treatment selection mechanism hold as well

title: Parallel trends in levels need not hold in logs
guidance: Because parallel trends is an assumption about averages of a particular transformation of the outcome, it is insensitive to functional form only under conditions (random adoption or a constant outcome distribution) that are usually implausible. The choice between rates, logs or other transformations is therefore itself an identifying assumption, and Roth and Sant'Anna provide a falsification test for it.
action: Record the outcome transformation used in each difference-in-differences study as an assumption, and treat alternative transformations as a principled dimension of a multiverse rather than an arbitrary one.
quote: there is no guarantee that parallel trends holds across different transformations

title: Covariate balance checks are indirect tests of parallel trends
guidance: Parallel trends is untestable because it concerns an unobserved counterfactual, so tests are necessarily indirect: imbalance in observed determinants of untreated outcome trends (normalised differences above roughly 0.25) suggests it may fail. Baseline levels are not differenced out if they are related to trends, and imbalance in covariate changes is informative only for covariates the treatment cannot affect.
action: Look for a balance table on determinants of outcome trends, in both levels and changes, and note whether the authors classify each covariate as exogenous or as a possible mechanism.
quote: Assumption PT is fundamentally untestable, as it contains an unobserved counterfactual component. Therefore, "tests" of these assumptions are necessarily indirect

title: Time-varying controls in two-way fixed effects mean controlling for changes
guidance: In a two-period panel, including a time-varying covariate in a fixed effects regression amounts to controlling for its change, whereas baseline levels can only matter if interacted with the post-period indicator. The regression specification thus silently determines which conditional parallel trends assumption is imposed, and covariates affected by the treatment are bad controls that bias the estimate.
action: For each difference-in-differences study with covariates, identify whether controls enter as levels, changes or post-period interactions, and whether any could be affected by treatment.
quote: Controlling for annual poverty rates really means controlling for poverty changes, and areas that are poor are not the same as areas that are becoming poor.

title: Regression with covariates identifies the effect only if effects are homogeneous
guidance: Even with correctly chosen and correctly specified covariates, the two-way fixed effects coefficient is a non-convex weighted average of covariate-specific effects plus misspecification bias terms, and can be negative when every stratum effect is positive. It recovers the average treatment effect on the treated only under the extra assumption that effects do not vary across covariate strata; regression adjustment, inverse probability weighting or doubly robust estimators avoid this.
action: When a paper reports a covariate-adjusted two-way fixed effects estimate, ask whether treatment effects plausibly vary with those covariates and whether a doubly robust estimate is also provided.
quote: (10) implicitly rules out that treatment effects can vary across covariate strata, which makes the weighting issues identified by Caetano and Callaway (2024) irrelevant to the interpretation

title: Pre-trends test the wrong periods and are often underpowered
guidance: Pre-treatment differential trends measure untreated outcome gaps before treatment, not in the post-treatment periods that the parallel trends assumption actually restricts. They are uninformative when measured too far before treatment or when selection depends on pretreatment shocks, and tests for them are typically too low-powered to rule out violations large enough to overturn the estimate; conditioning on passing such a test can worsen bias.
action: Do not accept a flat-looking event-study pre-period as proof of parallel trends; check the width of the pre-period confidence intervals against the size of the estimated effect.
quote: Under no anticipation, pre-trends do measure differences in untreated outcome trends between treated and untreated units, but they necessarily measure them in the "wrong" periods

title: Replace the eye-test with bounded sensitivity to parallel trends violations
guidance: Rather than informally judging whether pre-trends look flat, researchers should state how large a violation would be needed to explain the result (Bilinski and Hatfield) or bound the effect under a maximum post-period violation calibrated to pre-period estimates (Rambachan and Roth). In the Medicaid example the robust interval spans implausibly large effects in both directions, showing how little the pre-trends constrain.
action: Look for a Rambachan-Roth style sensitivity analysis or breakdown value in each difference-in-differences study, and treat its absence as a gap in the evidence for parallel trends.
quote: we caution producers (and consumers) of DiD work against the common practice of using only a simple "eye-test" for whether pre-trends differ substantially from zero

title: Staggered adoption multiplies the possible parallel trends assumptions
guidance: With several treatment cohorts, each group-time effect can be identified using never-treated units, not-yet-treated units, or by assuming parallel trends for all groups and periods; each choice is a different identifying assumption. The comparison group is therefore not a technical detail but the substantive assumption on which the estimate rests, and 'never treated' usually means 'not yet treated by the end of the data'.
action: Record for each staggered difference-in-differences study which comparison group (never-treated, not-yet-treated, or all) is used and treat alternative comparison groups as a principled multiverse dimension.
quote: Choosing which comparison groups to use to identify an ATT(g, t) is directly tied to which form(s) of parallel trends hold.

title: Two-way fixed effects uses already-treated units as controls with negative weights
guidance: In staggered designs, the two-way fixed effects estimand implicitly compares later-treated units with already-treated units, so it can place negative weight on some group-time effects even when parallel trends holds everywhere; it is unbiased only if effects do not change over time. The authors do not recommend it, noting that the problems are well understood and easily remedied by estimating the building blocks directly.
action: Where a field's difference-in-differences evidence rests on two-way fixed effects with staggered timing, check whether treatment effects plausibly evolve with exposure time and whether the authors also report a heterogeneity-robust estimator.
quote: Even if PT holds for all groups and all periods, the resulting estimand can actually put negative weight on certain ATT(g, t) parameters.

title: Eight forward-engineering steps for any difference-in-differences study
guidance: The recommended workflow is: define target parameters in potential-outcomes notation; state formally the parallel trends, no anticipation and overlap assumptions and gather evidence such as pretreatment trends; choose an estimation method and state its extra modelling restrictions; discuss what is treated as fixed versus random for inference; estimate; conduct sensitivity analysis against plausible violations; analyse heterogeneity; and switch designs if the assumptions are implausible.
action: Use these steps as the rubric for coding how completely each difference-in-differences study documents its parameter, assumptions, estimator, inference and sensitivity analysis.
quote: Be explicit about which form of these assumptions is required for identification in the study. Engage with the theoretical arguments necessary for them to hold and generate appropriate empirical evidence

title: Policing replication: directly challenging a named published paper
guidance: The authors propose a narrower replication category, policing replication, in the spirit of Merton's organized skepticism: a study that stress-tests a published result and engages with it directly in its title or abstract. Broader implicit replications are valuable but leave it to the reader to decide whether a prior claim has been tested.
action: When recording evidence against or for a finding, note whether the later study explicitly names and challenges the original, and give such tests more weight as scrutiny.
quote: The constitutive feature of a replication to qualify as policing, we argue, is the direct engagement with the original work in the title or the abstract.

title: Under one percent of top economics papers police earlier work
guidance: Screening all 29,682 papers in the top 50 economics journals from 2010 to 2020, the authors identified 259 policing replications, 0.9 percent of output. Most published findings in the field therefore have never been directly challenged in print.
action: Default to the assumption that a focal finding has not been independently scrutinised unless a policing replication is found.
quote: 259 (or 0.9%) of all 29,682 published papers in the Top 50 economics journals between 2010 and 2020 fit our definition

title: Questionable practices offer latitude for rationalization
guidance: Questionable research practices are rarely blatantly improper; they offer latitude for rationalization and self-deception and include p-hacking, ex-post theorizing, underpowered results, uncorrected multiple testing and coding errors. Policing replications are designed to uncover such practices whether purposeful or unintentional.
action: List the specific questionable practices a design is exposed to (multiple testing, post hoc hypotheses, low power, coding) as separate risk entries rather than one generic flag.
quote: questionable research practices are not “blatantly improper” but “offer considerable latitude for rationalization and self-deception”

title: Pre-analysis plans need policing to improve credibility
guidance: Citing Ofosu and Posner, the authors note that whatever the theoretical benefits of preregistration, pre-analysis plans are unlikely to enhance credibility unless someone checks the plan against the analysis actually done. Transparency instruments deliver value only when paired with a culture of verification.
action: When a design is preregistered, record whether anyone has compared the plan to the reported analysis; absent that, do not upgrade its credibility.
quote: whatever the benefits of pre-registration may be in theory, PAPs are unlikely to enhance research credibility without vigorous policing

title: Data sharing matters only if someone takes the data to the test
guidance: Economics has made tremendous progress on availability of data and code, and stricter sharing policies already encourage better conduct, but deep and sustainable incentives for credible research emerge only when a replication culture uses the shared materials. Availability is a precondition for trust, not a warrant.
action: Treat open data and code as enabling verification rather than as evidence of verification; note whether anyone has actually reanalysed the materials.
quote: deep and sustainable incentives for credible research only emerge if, in parallel, a replication culture is established that takes the data to the test

title: Two replication rates: papers replicated versus papers that replicate
guidance: A replication rate can mean how many published papers have been replicated (the selective approach, focused on influential studies) or how many published papers are themselves replications (the total approach). The two answer different questions and yield very different numbers.
action: When citing a field's replication rate, state which of the two denominators it uses.
quote: the replication rate can measure two things: first, how many published papers are replicated. Or, second, how many published papers conduct a replication.

title: Replications were 0.1 percent of top-journal output over four decades
guidance: Mueller-Langer and colleagues, applying a narrow definition to all papers in the top 50 journals, found 130 replications among 126,505 papers published between 1974 and 2014. Broader definitions used in other reviews reach rates up to 60 percent, so reported rates depend almost entirely on definition.
action: Interpret any claimed replication rate relative to its definition, and use the narrow-definition figure as the realistic base rate of direct scrutiny.
quote: They find 130 replications in all 126,505 published papers between 1974 and 2014 (0.1%)

title: The burden of proof lies with the replicator
guidance: Re-emphasising Clemens, the authors hold that a replication must demonstrate that it should have obtained identical results to the original; it is the replicating authors who must justify the comparison. Clarity about whether a new paper speaks to the veracity of an earlier one should not be left to readers or coders.
action: When a later study is used as evidence against a finding, check that it establishes comparability with the original design before counting it as a failed replication.
quote: “the burden of proof [for] a study to demonstrate that it should have obtained identical results to the original” is with the authors of the (potential) replication

title: A policing replication investigates; the community judges
guidance: The authors use policing in a positive sense: the police investigate and compile evidence but do not sentence; the roles of prosecutor and court belong to the scientific community as readership. A replication therefore supplies evidence to update beliefs, not a verdict on the original.
action: Present replication results on the map as evidence with stated strength, leaving the overall verdict on a prediction to the aggregated evidence base.
quote: The police do not sentence. The police only investigate and compile evidence for a case.

title: Policing replications cluster in two journals and few fields
guidance: Of 42 journals, three published no policing replication since 2010 and 30 published fewer than five, while the American Economic Review and the Journal of Applied Econometrics account for almost half; replications concentrate in macro, financial and behavioural economics, with very few in development, environmental, health and labour economics.
action: When a field or subfield is mapped, note the scarcity of policing replications in applied fields as a structural gap in its evidence base.
quote: two journals (the AER and the Journal of Applied Econometrics) account for almost 50% of all published policing replications

title: Comments in the AER fell from 10-20 percent to 2-3 percent
guidance: Comments in the American Economic Review, which challenge earlier papers in the journal, declined from 10 to 20 percent of papers in the 1980s and 1990s to below 5 percent in the early 2010s and 2 to 3 percent recently, while the number of empirical papers rose; the share of empirical comments among empirical papers has thus fallen sharply.
action: Do not read the absence of published challenges to an influential finding as evidence that it has withstood scrutiny.
quote: there is a continuous downward sloping trend of comments in total, from a high level of between 10 and 20% of all papers

title: Most editors say they publish replications, but few say so publicly
guidance: In a survey, 79 percent of responding top-50 journal editors said they publish policing replications of papers from their own journal and 62 percent of those also of papers from elsewhere, yet only 17 percent of journal websites state that replications are considered. Stated openness is not matched by visible policy.
action: When assessing whether a finding could have been challenged, consider the publication outlets available for replications in that field at the time.
quote: The majority of editors, 79%, stated that their journal publishes policing replications of papers originally published in their own journal.

title: Overturn bias: mostly unsuccessful replications get published
guidance: Given current incentives and publication culture, replications that overturn a finding are far more likely to be published than confirmatory ones, a pattern documented in economics and psychology. The published record of replications is therefore not a random sample of replication attempts.
action: When tallying replication outcomes for a prediction, note that published failures are overrepresented and unpublished confirmations may exist.
quote: it is likely that, given the current incentive structure and replication publication culture in economics, mostly unsuccessful replications are published

title: Failed replications do not reduce citations of the original
guidance: Studies in psychology find that replications are largely neglected in citations and that even failed replications do not significantly reduce citations to the original paper; most economics journals do not even link replications from the original paper's page. Citation counts therefore carry no information about whether a finding survived scrutiny.
action: Link every replication to its target on the map explicitly, since the literature's own citation structure will not do it.
quote: replications are mostly neglected in terms of citations and even failed replications do not significantly reduce the citations of original papers

title: Methodological decisions trade off three kinds of inductive risk
guidance: Wilholt argues that every methodological decision balances the reliability of positive results, the reliability of negative results, and the investigation's power, understood as the rate at which it delivers definitive results. Which balance is correct depends on how the consequences of each possible outcome are valued, so what counts as being geared towards truth involves value judgments.
action: When mapping a design, record which error (false positive, false negative, or no result) its conventions are built to minimise, and at whose cost.
quote: Methodological decisions therefore typically involve a complex trade-off between the three risks of committing a false positive error, committing a false negative error, and ending up without any result at all.

title: Relying on results is weaker than believing them true
guidance: Scientists do not work from the assumption that published results are true; they remain prepared to challenge and test them when their own findings are unexpected. A well-designed collective enterprise keeps reliance weak enough that one person's mistake can be corrected by another's scrutiny.
action: Treat every mapped finding as provisional input that later designs are entitled to re-test rather than as a settled premise.
quote: The assumption that other scientists speak truly or even knowledgeably when they report their results would certainly be too strong.

title: Reliance presumes competence: right methods, skillfully applied
guidance: Sincerity alone is too weak a basis for epistemic reliance. Researchers additionally assume that colleagues chose the right methods for the problem, applied them skillfully and carefully, and drew conclusions attentive to all observations made. These competence assumptions are exactly what a map of designs and assumptions makes checkable.
action: For each design in the field, state explicitly what a reader must assume about method choice and execution to rely on its result.
quote: that they have chosen the right methods for the problem, that they have employed them skillfully and carefully, that they have drawn their conclusions with due attention to all the observations

title: No non-arbitrary universal reliability standard exists
guidance: Following Rudner and Douglas, Wilholt interprets the inductive-risk argument as showing that, from an individual researcher's perspective, there is no non-arbitrary correct level of reliability that applies across investigations, because the acceptable risk depends on how bad an error would be. Readers therefore cannot infer a fixed reliability from the mere fact that a result was published.
action: Do not assign a single credibility weight to all results in a field; ask what level of confirmation each design was built to deliver.
quote: there is no non-arbitrary way to determine a correct level of reliability that applies across a whole range of investigations

title: How sure we must be depends on how serious a mistake is
guidance: Evidence never provides conclusive support, so researchers must select a level of confirmation and declare it sufficient; statistics gives no guidance about that choice. The only rationally relevant facts are the evaluations of possible outcomes, as Rudner put it: how sure we need to be depends on how serious a mistake would be.
action: When judging whether a field's evidential threshold is reasonable, weigh the practical consequences of false positives and false negatives for the claim at issue.
quote: Inductive logic and the science of statistics provide no guidance as to the choice of this level.

title: Data exclusion, analysis and design choices all shift inductive risk
guidance: Beyond the final decision to report a result, choices about discarding measurements, how to analyse and interpret data, and how to design a study each affect the probability of a false result. Every yes-or-no decision that changes inductive risk ideally reflects the same utilities, so the whole chain of analytic choices embodies implicit value judgments.
action: Catalogue the exclusion, analysis and design choices of each study as risk-shifting decisions, not neutral technicalities.
quote: In deciding whether or not to discard a set of measurements from a particular run of an experiment, how to analyze and interpret a set of data, and even in settling the details of the design

title: Deeply embedded methodological decisions go undocumented
guidance: Many risk-relevant decisions are buried in the research process and are not explicitly documented, partly because some involve tacit judgment and partly because publications must compress information for the division of labour to work. Readers therefore cannot fully reconstruct the reliability a result aimed at from the published report.
action: Mark assumptions that depend on unreported analytic choices as unverifiable from the paper and seek code, data or multiverse evidence before weighting them.
quote: Many of the methodological decisions in question are deeply embedded within the research process and are often not explicitly documented and communicated in each individual case.

title: Mis-calibrated reliance either duplicates work or breeds dead ends
guidance: Reliance is a coordination problem: underestimating reliability leads to premature doubt and needless duplication, while overestimating it makes researchers cling to results longer than warranted and follow them into dead ends. The reliability producers aim at and the reliability users presuppose must be adapted to each other.
action: Calibrate credibility weights in the map to the reliability the original design plausibly targeted, neither dismissing nor over-trusting its results.
quote: When reliability is underestimated in acts of reliance, results of others will be called into doubt too early, leading to an unnecessary duplication of scientific work.

title: The 0.05 threshold is a coordinating convention, not an optimum
guidance: Wilholt treats the 0.05 significance convention as a solution to a coordination problem: a stricter level would make significant results more reliable but harder to obtain, a looser one the reverse, and no argument shows 0.05 is best. Its value lies in being widely recognised so that readers can gauge how far to rely on a reported significant effect.
action: Record the field's significance and reporting conventions as shared assumptions whose function is coordination, and note where studies deviate from them.
quote: One would be hard pressed to argue that 0.05 represents just the 'best' choice for facilitating a socially organized cognitive endeavor.

title: Rules about controls and data exclusion are community conventions
guidance: Decisions about experimental setup, analysis and interpretation are constrained by methodological rules shared within a research community, such as which controls a study should include, how to isolate an effect causally, and when data may be discarded. These rules are conventions that strike a balance between reliability and power rather than uniquely correct procedures.
action: Identify the field's conventional rules for controls and exclusions and treat departures from them, and the conventions themselves, as candidate assumptions to test.
quote: rules about what kind of controls a study should include, rules about what kind of precautions should be taken to causally isolate an experiment, rules about the conditions under which a set of data may be discarded

title: Raising reliability always costs power or more null results
guidance: Increasing the reliability of one kind of result is never unconditionally desirable because it raises the share of inconclusive investigations and possibly false negatives. Methodological standards therefore always strike an at least partly arbitrary balance, and what matters is that the balance they impose is common knowledge in the community.
action: When a field tightens a standard (for example stricter identification requirements), note the corresponding loss of definitive results and false-negative risk in the map.
quote: Methodological standards must always strike a balance between reliability and power, where 'power' signifies the rate at which a scientific investigation delivers definitive results.

title: Reliance means assuming professional methods suitably employed
guidance: What a relying scientist works into her plans is not a precise reliability figure but the assumption that results were produced by professional methods suitably employed, as defined by the conventional standards of the relevant community. Epistemic reliance is thus reliance on widespread observance of the rules of the trade.
action: When assessing testimony from a literature, ask whether each study visibly observed the field's rules of the trade, since that is what readers' reliance actually rests on.
quote: the assumption that the results she is relying upon were arrived at by means of professional methods suitably employed

title: Epistemic trust adds shared value judgments to reliance
guidance: Because standards leave gaps and not every decision is documented, users must estimate the utilities under which producers made their choices. When users and producers share a sense of the right evaluation of outcomes, reliance becomes genuine epistemic trust, and it is the presumption of shared values that makes coordination stable.
action: Make the field's implicit value judgments about which errors matter most explicit, so that readers can see whether their trust rests on shared or merely assumed values.
quote: reliance based on the presumption of shared ideas about the values of true results and the dangers inherent in errors

title: The aim of truth underdetermines the right error balance
guidance: Wilholt concludes that the correct balance between reliability and power, and between false negatives and false positives, is not fixed by the aim of truth alone. A collective enterprise needs an additional consensus on the benefits of being right and the costs of being wrong in each specific case.
action: Where a field disputes a design's credibility, check whether the disagreement is really about the acceptable error trade-off rather than about the evidence itself.
quote: The right balance between reliability and power, as well as the right balance between the risks of false negatives and false positives, are underdetermined by the aim of truth.

title: 66% to 90% of validity threats unaddressed in leadership research
guidance: Antonakis and colleagues coded 110 leadership articles from top journals against fourteen design and estimation conditions and found that researchers failed to address at least 66 percent and up to 90 percent of the conditions that make causal claims invalid. This is a field-level benchmark showing that the typical published design in management cannot support the causal claims it makes.
action: Expect that most causal claims in a management literature rest on unaddressed endogeneity threats, and audit each design against the fourteen threats.
quote: researchers fail to address at least 66% and up to 90% of design and estimation conditions that make causal claims invalid

title: If x is endogenous, its coefficient has no meaning at all
guidance: The authors insist that when a regressor correlates with the error term the coefficient cannot be interpreted even as an association: the true effect could be larger, smaller or of opposite sign. Standard hedges such as calling the result an association or acknowledging possible reverse causality do not rescue the estimate, so a map should not downgrade such findings to correlational evidence but flag them as uninterpretable.
action: When a design cannot establish exogeneity of the key regressor, record the estimate as uninterpretable rather than as weaker correlational support.
quote: If x is endogenous the coefficient of x simply has no meaning. The true coefficient could be higher, lower, or even of a different sign.

title: Causal analysis means modelling selection into treatment
guidance: Using the counterfactual framework, the paper explains that when treated and untreated groups differ on observed or unobserved characteristics, the counterfactual cannot be observed and the selection process must be modelled to recover consistent estimates. This defines what each quasi-experimental design on the map is trying to do and why non-equivalent group comparisons without a selection model fail.
action: For every non-randomised comparison in the field, record how (or whether) selection into the treatment group was modelled.
quote: Modeling this selection correctly is what causal analysis, in non-experimental settings, is all about.

title: Table 1: fourteen threats to validity as coding criteria
guidance: Table 1 lists the fourteen threats used to code the literature, grouped as omitted variables (omitted regressors, omitted fixed effects, unjustified random effects, non-exogenous regressors), omitted selection, simultaneity, measurement error, common-method variance, inconsistent inference (heteroscedasticity, clustering) and model misspecification. The table is a ready-made audit checklist for the assumptions behind any regression-based design.
action: Use the fourteen Table 1 threats as the assumption checklist attached to every regression-based design on the map.
quote: Note: The 14 threats to validity mentioned are the criteria we used for coding the studies we reviewed.

title: Omitted variables can flip the sign of other coefficients
guidance: Through algebra the paper shows that omitting a regressor correlated with x and with y folds that correlation into the estimated slope, and that all other regressors correlated with the omitted variable become inconsistent too; the bias can raise, lower or reverse signs. This is why the set of control variables is a substantive assumption rather than a cosmetic choice and belongs among the dimensions varied in a multiverse.
action: Treat the control set as an identifying assumption and vary it in the multiverse, noting which theoretically required controls the field routinely omits.
quote: this bias can increase or decrease remaining coefficients or change their signs!

title: Model fixed effects in nested or longitudinal data
guidance: With observations nested in firms or repeated over time, unobserved entity-level constants pooled into the error term create omitted variable bias whenever they correlate with the level-one regressors, which the authors consider likely. Including fixed effects via dummies or cluster means removes this at the cost of not estimating level-two predictors; random effects are acceptable only after a Hausman test shows they agree with the fixed-effects estimates.
action: Check whether panel or multilevel studies in the field include entity fixed effects or justify random effects with a Hausman test, and flag those that do neither.
quote: If the fixed effects correlating with Level 1 variables are not modeled, Level 1 estimates will be inconsistent to the extent that they correlate with the fixed effects (which is likely).

title: Non-representative or range-restricted samples attenuate estimates
guidance: Separate from selection into treatment, non-representative participation, range restriction and censored samples distort observed variability and bias estimates, as when IQ effects are estimated in a high-IQ sample or managers choose which subordinates rate them. The authors state that samples must be representative and random or the selection process must be modelled, which makes sample restrictions explicit assumptions to record and vary.
action: Document each study's sample restrictions and participant selection mechanism and treat unmodelled self-selection as a threat to the estimate.
quote: ideally, samples must be representative and random (and for all types of studies, whether correlational or testing for group differences); if they are not, the selection process must be modeled

title: Common-method variance biases estimates in either direction
guidance: When independent and dependent variables come from the same rater or method, a common unmeasured cause can bias the coefficient upward or downward, not only inflate it, and the popular latent method-factor correction cannot recover the true effect because the modeler does not know how the unmeasured cause operates. The authors argue the misspecified model can still pass fit tests, so good fit is no evidence that the method problem is absent.
action: Flag same-source designs as an unaddressed threat regardless of model fit, and note whether instruments or separate sources were used.
quote: the common source/method problem does not only inflate estimates as most researchers believe; it could bias them upwards as well as downwards

title: Controlling for everything is infeasible; use other identification
guidance: Statistical adjustment only yields consistent estimates when every source of variance in y is known and observed, which the authors call impractical and not recommended as a stand-alone strategy. All known theoretical controls must be included, but because unknown omitted causes are likely, consistency must also be secured through quasi-experimental methods such as instruments, regression discontinuity, difference-in-differences or selection models.
action: Do not accept a rich control set alone as evidence of identification; look for an exogenous source of variation in the design.
quote: Controlling for all sources of variance in the context of social science, though, is not feasible because the researcher has to identify everything that causes variation in y

title: Conditions for a valid instrument
guidance: An instrument is an exogenous source of variance that strongly predicts the endogenous regressor, affects the outcome only through it, and is unrelated to the error term; there must be at least as many instruments as endogenous variables, one must be excluded from the second stage, and instruments should be strongly related to x. With more instruments than endogenous variables the overidentifying restrictions can be tested.
action: For each instrumental-variable study on the map, record the relevance, exclusion and exogeneity arguments separately and whether an overidentification test was possible.
quote: The coefficient of x could be interpreted causally if an exogenous source of variance, say z, were found that strongly predicts x and is related to y via x only, and unrelated to e

title: Instruments need a theoretical overidentification test first
guidance: Even with overidentifying restrictions, the empirical test will not necessarily catch a bad instrument if all instruments share the same omitted cause; the authors therefore require instruments to pass a theoretical exogeneity argument before the empirical test and urge researchers to obtain more instruments than endogenous variables so the test can be run. Passing a statistical test is not sufficient evidence that the exclusion restriction holds.
action: Judge an instrument primarily on the theoretical argument for its exogeneity, and treat a passed overidentification test as supporting but not decisive evidence.
quote: the instruments must first pass a "theoretical overidentification" test before an empirical one

title: Regression discontinuity: selection on an observed cut-off
guidance: In the regression discontinuity design, assignment to treatment is determined by an explicitly observed threshold on a continuous variable that is included in the regression, so the error term contains no information correlated with the grouping variable. The authors show with simulations that it recovers the experimental treatment effect almost exactly, provided the assignment variable is modelled and, ideally, the interaction with the cut-off is included.
action: When a field uses threshold-based assignment, check that the running variable is modelled in the estimation and that the cut-off was not manipulable.
quote: in the RDD selection is due to a specific cut-off (or threshold) that is observed explicitly and modeled as such

title: Difference-in-differences rests on stable group differences over time
guidance: The difference-in-differences model compares a treated group with a comparable control group before and after an exogenous shock, differencing out contemporaneous confounders; the treatment effect is the group-by-time interaction. The key assumption is that the interaction is not endogenous: group differences would have been stable absent treatment and the timing of treatment is exogenous, which can be checked against pre-treatment trends, and standard errors must be clustered on the panel variable.
action: For each difference-in-differences study, record whether pre-treatment trends were compared, whether treatment timing was plausibly exogenous, and whether errors were clustered.
quote: that the difference between the groups is stable over time and that the timing of the treatment is exogenous

title: Ten commandments of causal analysis
guidance: The paper closes with ten best practices: include adequate controls or use instruments, model fixed effects in panel data, ensure regressors are exogenous, correct for non-random selection, use overidentification tests, correct for measurement error, avoid common-method bias, use robust and cluster-robust standard errors by default, correlate disturbances of endogenous mediators, and prefer limited-information estimators unless a Hausman test justifies full-information ones. The authors stress that design rules and statistics cannot fix an inadequate design.
action: Score each design against the ten commandments and present the unmet items as the explicit assumptions the field's causal claims depend on.
quote: simply put, design rules (Shadish & Cook, 1999); only when the design is adequate can appropriate statistical procedures be used to obtain consistent estimates

title: A valid instrument must satisfy three separate conditions
guidance: Beyond the ordinary least squares assumptions, an instrument is valid only if it is relevant (strongly predicts the endogenous predictor), (as if) random (uncorrelated with omitted causes of the outcome), and excludable (affects the outcome only through the instrumented predictor). The authors deliberately keep (as if) randomness and the exclusion restriction apart because, under heterogeneous effects, they are distinct assumptions that each need their own justification.
action: When mapping an instrumental-variable study, record how the paper argues each of the three conditions separately rather than accepting a single blanket claim of exogeneity.
quote: an IV z must also satisfy three conditions to qualify as a valid instrument: (1) relevance, (2) (as if) randomness, and (3) the exclusion restriction

title: Violating any one condition makes the instrumental-variable estimate inconsistent
guidance: The Monte Carlo simulation shows that when all three conditions hold, the instrumental-variable estimator centres on the true effect while ordinary least squares is biased by about 50 percent; but when a single condition fails, the instrumental-variable estimates are inconsistent and often further from the truth than ordinary least squares. Strong support for one condition cannot compensate for a weak case on another.
action: Treat an instrumental-variable design as credible only if every condition is defensible; flag the weakest condition as the design's binding assumption.
quote: the violation of just one of the three necessary conditions leads to inconsistent IV estimates

title: Check the first-stage F-statistic for excluded instruments only
guidance: Relevance is the one condition that can be tested directly, but the test is often done wrong: the reported F-statistic must cover only the excluded instruments, not all first-stage covariates including controls, and its degrees of freedom should be reported so readers can judge it. A significant bivariate correlation between instrument and predictor is not sufficient evidence of relevance.
action: When auditing a published instrumental-variable study, locate the excluded-instrument F-statistic and its degrees of freedom and compare it with Stock and Yogo critical values rather than the rule of thumb of 10.
quote: researchers must take great care to report the F-statistic of only the instrumental variable(s), rather than the F-statistic of all first-stage covariates including the controls

title: The (as if) random condition cannot be tested empirically
guidance: Because the error term is unobservable, no statistical test can establish that an instrument is uncorrelated with omitted variables. The condition must be argued from theory, intuition or institutional knowledge, supported where possible by balance checks on observables, which still say nothing about unobservables.
action: Map (as if) randomness as a theoretical assumption of the design and judge the quality of the argument offered, not whether a test was passed.
quote: it is impossible to empirically test whether the (as if) random condition holds because the error term of an equation (and thus its relation to z) is unobservable

title: A zero instrument-outcome correlation does not show exclusion
guidance: The exclusion restriction says the instrument affects the outcome only through the instrumented predictor; it does not require that the instrument and the outcome be uncorrelated. If the instrument is relevant and the predictor has a true effect, the instrument will mechanically correlate with the outcome. Arguing exclusion from the absence of such a correlation is a misconception found in the leadership literature.
action: Reject arguments that an instrument is excludable merely because it is empirically unrelated to the outcome, and look for a substantive argument about alternative channels instead.
quote: if z is relevant and there is a true effect of x on y, then an instrument will mechanically correlate with the outcome even when the exclusion restriction is satisfied

title: Passing an overidentification test is only tentative evidence of exclusion
guidance: The Hansen-Sargan or similar overidentification test assumes at least one instrument is valid, constant causal effects, adequate power, and that all instruments are (as if) random; a set of equally invalid instruments can pass it. A non-significant result is therefore weak, conditional evidence that the exclusion restriction holds.
action: When a paper leans on an overidentification test, check whether its four preconditions are argued before treating the exclusion restriction as supported.
quote: a non-significant overidentification test allows tentatively concluding that the exclusion restriction is satisfied when (a) the sample size is sufficiently large, (b) constant causal effects are plausible, (c) authors can convincingly argue that at least one instrument is valid

title: Endogeneity tests are only informative when the instruments are valid
guidance: Tests such as Wu-Hausman compare an efficient but possibly inconsistent estimator with the instrumental-variable estimator; they cannot prove the absence of endogeneity and, with weak or invalid instruments, lack power to detect a difference. A non-significant endogeneity test obtained with poor instruments is not evidence that the predictor is exogenous.
action: Do not accept a non-significant endogeneity test as support for an ordinary least squares specification unless the instruments have first been shown to be strong and plausibly valid.
quote: When IV(s) are not valid, researchers should not rely on an endogeneity test to conclude that a variable is likely exogenous.

title: The reduced form is causal under (as if) randomness alone
guidance: Regressing the outcome directly on the instrument requires only the (as if) random condition to give a consistent causal estimate of the instrument's effect, even if relevance or exclusion fail. It cannot identify the channel, but it is a robust fallback and a useful diagnostic; the instrumental-variable estimate is the ratio of the reduced form to the first stage.
action: Ask whether the paper reports the reduced form, and treat it as the most defensible causal quantity when the exclusion restriction is doubtful.
quote: of the three conditions for a valid instrument, estimating the reduced form equation only requires (as if) randomness to obtain consistent estimates

title: Instrumental-variable estimates are local average treatment effects
guidance: An instrumental-variable estimate describes the effect of the predictor for the units whose value of the predictor was moved by the instrument, not the average effect in the full sample. This matters for generalization: different instruments identify effects for different subpopulations, and overidentification tests can reject valid instruments simply because each recovers a different local effect.
action: Record which subpopulation (the compliers for the particular instrument) a reported instrumental-variable effect applies to before comparing it with estimates from other designs.
quote: IV estimates do not reflect the effect of x on y for the full sample. Rather, they reflect a so-called 'local average treatment effect' (LATE)

title: Only 38 percent of leadership instrumental-variable studies reported a correct F-statistic
guidance: In a review of 77 instrumental-variable studies from top management journals, only 28 clearly reported the correct excluded-instrument F-statistic, a third did not report it at all, and 27 percent omitted its degrees of freedom. Relevance is the only directly testable condition, yet most published studies do not allow readers to verify it.
action: Expect that the majority of instrumental-variable studies in a management field will not let you verify instrument strength; code them as unverified rather than as satisfied.
quote: only 28 studies (38 %) clearly reported the correct F-statistic. However, many studies (34 %) did not at all report the first-stage F-statistic of the excluded instruments.

title: Only 16 percent of studies justified (as if) random instruments
guidance: The (as if) random condition was the most neglected: just 12 of 77 reviewed studies gave a theoretical justification, and 52 did not discuss it at all. The authors identify this silence as the greatest weakness in the field's use of instrumental variables, since the condition is untestable and can only be made credible by argument.
action: When a field's instrumental-variable evidence is mapped, mark the (as if) random assumption as unaddressed by default and upgrade it only where an explicit argument is given.
quote: The (as if) random condition was the most ignored condition. Only 12 studies (16 %) theoretically justified the (as if) randomness of their IVs

title: Most studies never discussed the exclusion restriction
guidance: Forty-three of the 77 reviewed studies did not discuss the exclusion restriction at all, others folded it into a vague exogeneity claim, and six argued it held because the instrument was empirically unrelated to the outcome, which is a logical error. Only a minority drew on established theory to argue why no alternative channel exists.
action: Score the exclusion restriction in each mapped study on whether alternative causal channels from instrument to outcome are explicitly considered and ruled out.
quote: the results were mixed with respect to the exclusion restriction, with most articles not discussing this condition at all (N = 43)

title: Individual differences fail (as if) randomness because of selection into roles
guidance: Traits such as sex, personality or age may be randomly distributed in the population, but people are not randomly assigned to organizations and leadership roles; organizations attract, select and retain certain types, so a trait correlates with other determinants of the outcome. The same logic makes internal organizational factors (for example, a change in chief executive) and personal experiences unsuitable instruments.
action: Challenge any instrument built from leader or follower traits, experiences or internal firm characteristics by asking what selection process placed those units in the sample.
quote: the (as if) random condition may not hold especially in organizational settings because individuals, along with their stable individual differences, are not randomly assigned to roles and organizations

title: Reporting checklist for an instrumental-variable study
guidance: A complete report gives a theoretical rationale for (as if) randomness and exclusion, the excluded-instrument F-value, an endogeneity test, an overidentification test where the model is overidentified, degrees of freedom for all tests, first- and second-stage coefficients for every specification, the exact estimator and software command, a comparison with an efficient estimator, the reduced form, and a critical discussion of limitations.
action: Use these items as the reporting rubric when coding whether a published instrumental-variable study gives readers enough to evaluate its assumptions.
quote: researchers must report the F-value of the excluded IVs, an endogeneity test, and an overidentification test when appropriate. For all tests, it is critical that the degrees of freedom are reported.

title: Only 59 percent of instrumental-variable articles could be replicated
guidance: Of 114 instrumental-variable articles published in three top political science journals between 2010 and 2022, only 71 had complete replication materials and 67 could be replicated, mostly because data were incomplete. Even in a field with data-sharing policies, roughly four in ten instrumental-variable results cannot be independently reproduced, which limits what readers can check about their assumptions.
action: Record whether each instrumental-variable study in your map has public data and code, since without them none of the diagnostics below can be verified.
quote: Out of 114 articles meeting this criterion, 71 have complete replication materials online, which is concerning in itself. We successfully replicated at least one primary IV result in 67 out of the remaining 71 articles.

title: Exogeneity bundles two distinct assumptions: unconfoundedness and exclusion
guidance: The instrumental-variable exogeneity assumption requires both that the instrument is randomly or quasi-randomly assigned (unconfoundedness) and that it has no direct effect on the outcome except through the treatment (exclusion restriction). The two are conceptually separate and should be argued separately, even though violations of either are observationally equivalent and cannot be told apart from the data.
action: When mapping an instrumental-variable design, list unconfoundedness and the exclusion restriction as two separate assumptions and note whether the paper justifies each.
quote: Conceptually, unconfoundedness and the exclusion restriction are two distinct assumptions and should be justified separately in a research design.

title: Weak first stages amplify small exogeneity violations into large bias
guidance: Because the instrumental-variable estimator is a ratio of the reduced form to the first stage, a near-zero first-stage covariance magnifies any small correlation between the instrument and the error term. The two assumption failures compound each other, so with invalid and weak instruments the asymptotic bias of two-stage least squares can greatly exceed that of ordinary least squares.
action: Treat a weak instrument as raising, not merely widening, the risk of a biased estimate, and weight such studies accordingly when assessing a field's evidence.
quote: the two identifying assumption failures exacerbate each other: having a weak first-stage compounds problems from confounding or exclusion restriction violations, and vice versa

title: Theory-justified instruments remain 60 percent of published designs
guidance: Instruments were classified by design strength: experiments (17 percent), rules and policy changes (10 percent), theory-based justifications such as weather, geography, history or diffusion (60 percent), and econometric constructions such as lags or shift-share (13 percent). The authors are sceptical of the theory category because many such instruments appear ad hoc or post hoc and do not genuinely uphold the assignment and exclusion assumptions.
action: Classify each instrument in the mapped field by how it was generated (experiment, rule, theory, econometric construction) and treat theory-based instruments as the weakest default.
quote: We remain skeptical because many "theory"-driven instruments, in our view, do not genuinely uphold these assumptions, often appearing to be developed in an ad hoc or post hoc manner.

title: Weather and geography instruments are quasi-random but rarely excludable
guidance: Authors often argue that rainfall, elevation or distance are imposed by nature and hence unconfounded, but it is much harder to argue that such variables affect political or economic outcomes only through the one treatment of interest; several mechanisms have been documented. Spatial instruments also face cross-sectional interdependence and simultaneity problems.
action: For any weather, climate or geographic instrument, enumerate the known alternative channels to the outcome before accepting the exclusion restriction.
quote: While authors often argue that weather or geography is quasi-randomly imposed, it is typically harder to claim they only affect the outcome through the treatment variable.

title: 17 percent of designs did not report a first-stage F-statistic
guidance: Among 70 replicated instrumental-variable designs, 12 did not report the first-stage partial F-statistic at all, and 9 of the 58 that did used classic analytic standard errors that ignore heteroskedasticity or clustering. The reported strength of an instrument therefore often cannot be taken at face value from the published paper.
action: Check whether the first-stage F-statistic is reported and which standard errors it is based on before accepting a claim that an instrument is strong.
quote: among the 70 IV designs, 12 (17%) do not report this crucial statistic despite its key role in justifying the validity of an IV

title: Clustering shrinks first-stage F; 11 to 17 percent of designs are weak
guidance: When the data have a clustering structure, the originally reported F-statistic tends to overstate instrument strength relative to the effective F-statistic of Olea and Pflueger or a bootstrapped F. Using the effective F, 8 of 70 designs (11 percent) fall below 10; with the bootstrapped F the share rises to 17 percent. Failure to cluster is a known problem for significance but has been neglected when judging instrument strength.
action: Recompute or request the effective F-statistic with cluster-robust standard errors for any instrumental-variable study with grouped data, and flag designs below 10 as weak.
quote: when a clustering structure exists, the original F-statistic tends to be larger than the effective F or bootstrapped F. When using the effective F as the benchmark, eight studies (11%) have FEff < 10.

title: Two-stage least squares standard errors are typically 3.8 times larger
guidance: In the replication sample the median ratio of two-stage least squares to ordinary least squares analytic standard errors was 3.8, falling as the first stage strengthens. To reach the same significance level, an instrumental-variable estimate must therefore be about three times larger than the ordinary least squares estimate, which creates an opening for publication bias and p-hacking toward inflated effects.
action: When an instrumental-variable estimate is both large and barely significant, consider selective reporting as a competing explanation to a genuine large effect.
quote: to achieve comparable levels of statistical significance, 2SLS estimates often need to be at least three times larger than OLS estimates

title: Robust inference overturns significance in 17 to 35 percent of designs
guidance: Only 10 percent of the original studies failed to reject the null at the 5 percent level, but with the Anderson-Rubin test 17 percent fail, with bootstrap methods 19 to 27 percent fail, and with the tF procedure for single-instrument designs 35 percent fail. Conventional t-tests with analytic standard errors systematically understate the uncertainty of two-stage least squares estimates.
action: Discount instrumental-variable results that rely solely on a conventional t-test, and look for Anderson-Rubin, bootstrap or tF-based inference before counting a result as significant.
quote: Using the AR test, we cannot reject the null hypothesis of no effect at the 5% level in 12 studies (17%), compared with 7 (10%) in the original studies.

title: 97 percent of two-stage least squares estimates exceed ordinary least squares
guidance: In 68 of 70 designs the instrumental-variable estimate was larger in magnitude than the naive ordinary least squares estimate, with a median ratio of 3.4 and a third at least five times larger, even though the usual rationale for the instrument is to remove upward bias and only 21 percent of authors expected downward bias. The ratio is strongly negatively related to instrument strength in observational studies but not in experimental ones, pointing to exogeneity violations rather than heterogeneity or measurement error.
action: Treat a large two-stage least squares to ordinary least squares ratio combined with a weak first stage as a warning sign that the exogeneity assumption is violated.
quote: in all but two designs (97%), the 2SLS estimates are bigger than the OLS estimates, consistent with Jiang's (2017) finding based on finance research

title: Heterogeneous effects cannot explain the instrumental-variable inflation
guidance: Thirty percent of replicated studies invoke heterogeneous treatment effects (compliers responding more strongly) to explain why the instrumental-variable estimate exceeds ordinary least squares. Decomposing the gap following Ishimaru shows that the variance in treatment effects required to produce the observed differences is implausibly large, so this defence should not be accepted without a profile of the complier population.
action: When a paper attributes an inflated instrumental-variable estimate to complier heterogeneity, ask for principal-strata profiling rather than accepting the claim.
quote: it is highly unlikely that heterogeneous treatment effects alone can explain the difference in magnitudes between 2SLS and OLS estimates we observe in the replication data

title: Many observational instrumental-variable results lack credibility or precision
guidance: Summarising the replications, observational designs have weaker first stages, larger increases in p-values under robust inference, and larger discrepancies from ordinary least squares than experimental designs. The authors conclude that a substantial share of observational instrumental-variable results either are not credible or are too imprecise to add anything beyond the ordinary least squares regression.
action: Give observational instrumental-variable evidence lower credibility weight than experiment-generated instruments when aggregating a field's findings.
quote: a significant proportion of IV results based on observational data in political science either lack credibility or yield estimates that are too imprecise to offer insights beyond those provided by OLS regressions

title: Checklist: effective F, robust inference, reduced form, and placebo tests
guidance: The recommended practice is to decide at design stage whether ordinary least squares bias even warrants an instrument; report the effective F-statistic with clustering but not discard a design solely because it is below 10; use tF or Anderson-Rubin inference when the first stage is weak; present ordinary least squares and instrumental-variable estimates with confidence intervals from several methods; report first-stage and reduced-form results; and where possible run a zero-first-stage placebo test and a sensitivity analysis.
action: Audit each instrumental-variable study against these items and, in a multiverse, vary the inferential method (analytic, bootstrap, Anderson-Rubin, tF) as a principled robustness dimension.
quote: Calculate and report FEff for the first stage, taking into account heteroscedasticity and clustering structure as needed. However, do not discard a design simply because FEff < 10.

title: Be alarmed when the instrument inflates an upward-biased estimate
guidance: If the stated reason for the instrument is that ordinary least squares overstates the effect, then an instrumental-variable estimate that is much larger than ordinary least squares contradicts the paper's own logic and signals an invalid instrument. The authors list this as a primary diagnostic, together with a placebo test among never-takers and a Cinelli-Hazlett sensitivity analysis.
action: Compare the paper's stated direction of ordinary least squares bias with the direction of the instrumental-variable correction, and flag any contradiction.
quote: If you expect the OLS results to be upward biased, be concerned if the 2SLS estimator yields much larger estimates than OLS.

title: Canonical difference-in-differences rests on parallel trends and no anticipation
guidance: In the two-period, two-group model, the average treatment effect on the treated is identified by two assumptions: that treated and comparison outcomes would have moved in parallel absent treatment, and that treatment has no effect before it is implemented. With many independent clusters, a two-way fixed effects regression consistently estimates this effect and clustered standard errors are valid; most recent methods relax one of these canonical components.
action: Map each difference-in-differences study by identifying which canonical assumption (timing, parallel trends, or sampling) its setting departs from.
quote: The key identifying assumption is that the average outcome among the treated and comparison populations would have followed ''parallel trends'' in the absence of treatment. We also assume that the treatment has no causal effect before its implementation (no anticipation).

title: Forbidden comparisons can give two-way fixed effects the wrong sign
guidance: With staggered adoption, a two-way fixed effects regression mixes clean comparisons of treated with not-yet-treated units and forbidden comparisons in which already-treated units serve as controls. Under heterogeneous effects, the resulting negative weights can make the coefficient take the opposite sign of every individual effect, and even positive weights need not correspond to a policy-relevant parameter.
action: For any staggered difference-in-differences study estimated by two-way fixed effects, check whether treatment effects could vary across cohorts or over time and whether a heterogeneity-robust estimator is reported.
quote: these ''forbidden'' comparisons potentially lead to severe drawbacks such as TWFE coefficients having the opposite sign of all individual-level treatment effects due to ''negative weighting'' problems

title: Practitioner checklist: timing, parallel trends, and clustering
guidance: The checklist asks three questions. If units are not all treated at once, use a heterogeneity-robust estimator unless willing to restrict effect heterogeneity. If parallel trends is uncertain, condition on covariates where that helps, plot an event study, report the power of the pre-test or a non-inferiority test, and report formal sensitivity analysis. For inference, cluster at the level at which treatment is independently assigned, or use few-cluster or design-based methods.
action: Score each mapped difference-in-differences study against these checklist items to locate where its evidence for its assumptions is thin.
quote: Use TWFE only if you're willing to restrict treatment effect heterogeneity.

title: Dynamic event-study coefficients are contaminated across cohorts
guidance: Adding leads and lags to a two-way fixed effects regression yields interpretable dynamic effects only if the effect at each horizon is the same across adoption cohorts. Otherwise the coefficient at one lag absorbs effects from other lags and some units receive negative weight, and crucially the pre-treatment lead coefficients may be non-zero even when parallel trends holds, making pre-trend assessments from such regressions misleading.
action: Treat pre-trend plots built from dynamic two-way fixed effects regressions with staggered timing as unreliable evidence for or against parallel trends.
quote: the ''treatment lead'' coefficients from (7) are not guaranteed to be zero even if parallel trends is satisfied in all periods (and vice versa), and thus evaluation of pre-trends based on these coefficients can be very misleading

title: Diagnostics for how much two-way fixed effects relies on bad comparisons
guidance: Several diagnostics quantify the aggregation problem: the share of group-time effects receiving negative weight and the heterogeneity needed to flip the sign (de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille), the Goodman-Bacon decomposition of the coefficient into two-by-two comparisons and the weight on already-treated controls, and tests of constant effects (Jakiela). The authors regard removing bad comparisons as better than merely diagnosing them.
action: When a mapped study retains two-way fixed effects, look for a weight decomposition or negative-weight diagnostic and record how much weight falls on already-treated comparisons.
quote: propose reporting the number/fraction of group-time ATTs that receive negative weights, as well as the degree of heterogeneity in treatment effects that would be necessary for the estimated treatment effect to have the ''wrong sign''

title: Heterogeneity-robust estimators differ by comparison group and baseline period
guidance: Estimators such as Callaway and Sant'Anna, Borusyak-Jaravel-Spiess, Sun and Abraham, and stacked regressions all aggregate clean two-by-two comparisons but differ in whether they use never-treated or not-yet-treated units and whether they use only the last pre-period or all pre-periods. Using longer horizons is more efficient but more exposed to approximate parallel trends violations. They usually, though not always, give similar answers.
action: Record the comparison group and baseline period of each estimator used, and treat switching between these choices as a principled multiverse dimension rather than a free specification choice.
quote: The first-order consideration is therefore to use an approach that makes clear what the target parameter is and which groups are being compared for identification.

title: Parallel trends is sensitive to the functional form of the outcome
guidance: If parallel trends holds in levels it generally fails in logs and vice versa; it holds for all monotone transformations only when the population splits into an as-good-as-randomly assigned group and a group with a stable outcome distribution, which rarely describes settings where difference-in-differences is used. The choice of outcome scale is thus part of the identifying assumption and should be justified.
action: Check whether a difference-in-differences paper justifies its choice of outcome scale and whether results are reported for alternative transformations.
quote: If parallel trends holds using the outcome measured in levels, Yi,t (0), then it will generally not be the case that it holds for the outcomes measured in logs

title: Parallel pre-trends do not guarantee parallel post-trends
guidance: Even exactly parallel pre-treatment trends do not ensure the counterfactual post-treatment trends were parallel: boys' and girls' heights grow in parallel until thirteen and then diverge, yet bar mitzvahs do not cause growth. Pre-trends are informative but are not the assumption itself, so the plausibility of parallel trends must also be argued from context.
action: Ask whether the paper gives a substantive reason, independent of the pre-trend plot, to expect both groups to have trended alike in the post-period.
quote: even if pre-trends are exactly parallel, this need not guarantee that the post-treatment parallel trends assumption is satisfied

title: Pre-trend tests often miss violations as large as the estimated effect
guidance: A linear violation of parallel trends that a pre-trend test detects only half the time will also produce a spurious significant effect half the time. In simulations calibrated to papers in three leading economics journals, Roth found that violations detectable only 50 percent of the time frequently produce biases as large as or larger than the reported treatment effect. Conditioning on passing the test adds a further pre-test selection bias.
action: Discount an insignificant pre-trend as evidence for parallel trends unless the paper also reports the power of that test against economically relevant violations.
quote: linear violations of parallel trends that conventional tests would detect only 50% of the time often produce biases as large as (or larger than) the estimated treatment effect

title: Non-inferiority pre-tests reverse the burden of proof
guidance: Standard pre-tests take parallel trends as the null and only reject with strong evidence, so failing to reject proves little. Non-inferiority approaches (Bilinski and Hatfield; Dette and Schumann) instead take a large pre-trend as the null and reject only when the data show the pre-trend is small, guaranteeing power against large violations, though they still do not deliver valid confidence intervals for the treatment effect.
action: Prefer studies that test the null of a large pre-trend, or at least report what magnitude of pre-trend their test could have detected.
quote: rather than test the null that pre-treatment trends are zero, they test the null that the pre-treatment trend is large, and reject only if the data provides strong evidence that the pre-treatment trend is small

title: Report the breakdown value for parallel trends violations
guidance: Rambachan and Roth bound the post-treatment violation of parallel trends relative to the largest pre-treatment violation and construct confidence sets valid under that bound; the resulting breakdown value states how large a violation (as a multiple of the pre-period maximum) would be needed to overturn the conclusion. Unlike pre-tests, these sets widen when pre-trends are imprecisely estimated. Such sensitivity analysis should become standard alongside event-study plots.
action: Record each study's breakdown value where reported, and treat its absence as leaving the parallel trends assumption unquantified.
quote: how big would the post-treatment violation of parallel trends have to be relative to the largest pre-treatment violation to invalidate a particular conclusion?

title: Interpret robustness using context-specific knowledge of confounds
guidance: A conclusion robust to violations twice the pre-period maximum is strong if other factors were stable around treatment but weak if treatment coincided with a shock larger than anything in the pre-period, such as a recession. Formal sensitivity tools must be combined with a discussion of what time-varying factors could have differentially affected the treated group.
action: Pair each difference-in-differences study's sensitivity results with a note on contemporaneous shocks in its setting before judging the credibility of its parallel trends assumption.
